It also proposes four categories — capabilities, resources, evaluation and deployment — and asks that no single recursive system holds research, evaluation, resource and deployment rights at once.

Beyond policy proposals, technical research on RSI safety has also started to appear in academic discourse. A group of researchers from leading Chinese universities and research institutes measured how much of AI research AI already does. They logged 769 tasks from the development of its own agentic research model and found that AI was involved in 96.5% of tasks and proposed most methods, but humans made the final choice in 85.5% of method decisions.

These Chinese researchers also argued that authority over human safety needs to be handled seriously, and each advance in AI capability should be matched by investment in alignment and oversight, with clear rules on whose goals AI pursues and who remains accountable. Similar work is multiplying: The Chinese Academy of Sciences has proposed studying the “evolutionary safety” of recursively self-improving AI; Shanghai AI Lab has explored using RSI itself to improve safety (“recursive safety improvement”) and documented how self-evolving agents “misevolve.”

Overall, the discussion of RSI and its safety in China resembles a bottom-up effort. AI companies, AI governance scholars, and technical safety researchers talk about it most often, while top-level policy is gradually catching up as the topic becomes more prominent in AI discourse. There is little public evidence that the top leadership treats RSI as a priority. But the broader AI community, from AI companies to AI governance scholars and research communities, is becoming more vocal about it, which may inform and influence thinking at the top.

Chinese AI companies disclose details about AI R&D automation

Thinking about RSI risks in China is still at an early stage. However, one basis for governing RSI is already partly in place: disclosure. People need to know what AI is actually doing inside AI labs to set rules. Chinese AI companies have already started to publish about where and how they use AI in their research.

Firstly, they disclose where they apply AI in the research pipeline in order to showcase their models’ automated research capabilities. MiniMax reports that M2.7 is capable of constructing complex Agent Harness on its own. It has also described agents that “help with literature review, track a pre-set experiment spec, pipeline data and other artifacts, and launch experiments” in an RL scenario.

Xiaomi introduced CodeMidas, “an agentic pipeline that turns implemented functionality in existing codebases into executable RL environments using source code as its only task-specific input.” It resulted in “5,545 training tasks from 3,185 open-source codebases spanning 23 programming languages and 15 technical domains.” Z.ai’s “Toward Recursive Self-Improvement” blog post states that its GLM-5.3-powered Infra Agent helped build the inference system that serves GLM-5.3-Flash on more than 100,000 Chinese-made accelerators, chips designed for AI computation.

RSI direction: Firms (linked to examples)

Overall research workflow: MiniMax, ByteDance Seed (Seed for Seed), Alibaba (Iris)
Harness: MiniMax
Training data / RL environments: Xiaomi, DeepSeek, Z.ai, Moonshot, Alibaba (Qwen3), Alibaba (Qwen-UI-Agent), Tencent Hunyuan (using DeepSeek’s model though)
Training / inference infrastructure: Z.ai, Moonshot, MiniMax, ByteDance Seed (CUDA Agent)

They also describe how the AI did the work and what it achieved. According to MiniMax’s announcement in March 2026, MiniMax’s M2.7 ran a loop of more than 100 rounds on an internal harness and reported a 30% gain on an internal evaluation set. In this process, M2.7 studied failed attempts, planned changes, edited the harness code, reran the evaluation, and made decisions on whether to keep the change. Moonshot’s Kimi K3 report (July 2026, revised August) says agents built its training tasks and the starting workspaces for its personal-assistant tasks, and that earlier Kimi models wrote its fine-tuning data.

Z.ai’s blog post in September 2026, “Toward Recursive Self-Improvement,” mentions the division of labor during building infrastructure: “Engineers defined objectives and system boundaries. The agent handled analysis, hypotheses, and code changes. The experimental environment provided layered, timely, and verifiable feedback.” Z.ai says the work, much of which it credits to the agent, tripled end-to-end throughput relative to the initial baseline.

By contrast, OpenAI and Anthropic mostly publish aggregate usage statistics, often oriented toward risk assessment. Anthropic says Claude wrote more than 80% of the code it merged (May 2026), and “leads” 26% of its AI R&D work (August 2026). OpenAI does break agents’ output down by research task, but only as token counts.

Of course, OpenAI and Anthropic also sometimes report more details. For example, OpenAI’s blog post introducing GPT-5.5 this April says Codex analyzed weeks of production traffic and wrote new load-balancing rules for serving, which made token generation over 20% faster. Anthropic has mentioned that in an experiment, Claude Sonnet 5 spent 60 hours trying to fix alignment failures in an early checkpoint of Claude Opus 4.8 by creating training data.

But overall, in our assessment, Chinese AI companies seem to be a bit more detailed about AI R&D automation applications. Part of this contrast comes from the fact that Chinese AI companies are more open and thus publish more technical reports reporting the AI’s process step by step.

Policy implications

Our findings suggest that RSI in China, so far, looks less like a state-led geopolitical race than a bottom-up, commercially driven trend.

First, Chinese companies do not even share a language for it. They picked up “RSI” only recently, largely following discussions in Silicon Valley, and still use the term to mean different things. Second, one visible driver is commercial: RSI helps with fundraising, aims at easing compute constraints in the future, and shows investors efficiency gains.. Third, RSI barely features in policy. Its only appearance in an official document treats it as a trend to watch with “vigilance,” and prominent voices in party-affiliated media emphasize keeping it under human control. Fourth, Chinese companies already disclose some details about how they use AI in research, which gives outside observers more to work with than the race narrative suggests.

The public evidence does not support the claim that China is racing to reach RSI first. Commercial incentives and competitive market dynamics can encourage Chinese AI companies to double down on research automation without explicit policy instruction or geopolitical racing dynamics. Therefore, regardless of geopolitical calculations, the world must prepare for a scenario in which automation of AI research happens more aggressively in leading AI labs in both countries.

One should therefore focus on understanding the capabilities being developed in leading labs in both countries. Before pursuing ambitious international agreements, researchers, companies, and policymakers could take two basic but necessary steps.

First, scientists and AI researchers from both countries could develop a shared vocabulary that distinguishes among the automation of individual research tasks, closed feedback loops, and systems that produce self-sustaining acceleration in capabilities. Exchanges could help establish what each side means by terms such as “automating AI research,” “self-evolution,” and “recursive self-improvement.” Using these terms to describe very different processes obscures the risks involved and makes it harder to identify appropriate safeguards.

Second, companies could adopt common transparency standards. Reports should specify which research tasks AI performs, how its performance is evaluated, how often humans intervene, how much AI accelerates different parts of and overall AI research, what decisions remain under human control, and what safeguards prevent systems from altering their own records or authorizing their own deployment. Chinese and American companies have already disclosed some information about their use of AI in research, which provides a limited foundation for more systematic reporting. Independent evaluations and tamper-resistant logs would make such disclosures more credible and comparable.

U.S. labs could build on what Chinese companies already do by publishing clearer, more detailed accounts of how they automate research. Chinese companies, in turn, could go beyond stating that humans remain in the loop and specify the safeguards actually in place to govern increasingly autonomous systems. Greater transparency about AI R&D automation would give researchers on both sides a concrete basis for engagement. This does not require unrestricted disclosure of sensitive research, or either side adopting the other’s standards wholesale. Converging on a common reporting baseline would support information exchange and help both sides assess emerging capabilities and risks without relying on vague claims or geopolitical speculation.

Zilan Qian is a research scholar at GovAI researching AI development and regulation in China.

Cheryl Wu is a research scholar at GovAI researching Chinese AI landscape and economics of AI.

1

Selective examples, not exhaustive.

2

Data from Pitchbook

3

According to Standard AI Index 2026, in generative AI, U.S. private investment in generative AI is around 23 times that of China.

4

Study Times is published by the Central Party School, the Communist Party of China’s highest internal training institution. An article there is not a formal statement of policy, but it signals that the topic is considered legitimate and relevant for officials to think about.

5

A media outlet managed and sponsored by local state-owned enterprises

item.title: Behind the scenes of those Claude slopcore music videos
item.description: The hottest new music video director is Opus 5.5.
item.content:encoded:
By Clara Collier

If you’ve spent any amount of time on Twitter recently (oops), you’ll have noticed that the hottest new music video director is Claude Opus 5.5. You may also have noticed one account whose videos stand out against the tide of clay-orange-accented, screen-text-heavy slop. They feature cinematic visuals, dense, witty references to hyperspecific corners of internet culture, and a refreshing absence of dancing anime girls. Instead, the singer is “Claudia” — apparently, an elfin 20-something with a black bob and a tasteful orange streak; in fact, a product of Midjourney, Seedance, and the imagination of RJ Tevonian, known on Twitter as anabology.

When I first watched Tevonian’s videos, I was overcome with dread for the human film industry. I also had to know how he did it. Fortunately, he agreed to an interview. Below, we talk about his process, what it’s like to fight Claude, the future of human-generated media, and whether “slopcore” has the makings of a real genre.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity. All images courtesy of RJ Tevonian.

Clara Collier: How did you get started making these music videos?

RJ Tevonian: Honestly, I don’t have a huge history in it. My main thing is that I run a biotech company. But I think two things got me into this. One, I’ve spent so much of my time building really complicated AI setups where I make everything super streamlined. So when I saw people making AI music videos with Claude, I thought, well, I feel like I could do that.

Second, I have some history in dance. Not really music, classically, but dance. And through creating concepts in dance, freestyle-type stuff, I learned how to parameterize a design space, where you can create concepts almost algorithmically, once you figure out how to define a concept well enough.

So then I wondered if I could do this with other types of design. I made all these tools to distill my design taste into a computer: I was able to pull a bunch of mood boards from online, compare two pictures against each other, and select the one I liked. Over time, the computer could learn rules about what my visual taste was. I had the idea that design should be better parameterized, and I’d been trying to do that for probably a few weeks before this trend showed up. Then I saw that some other people were making AI music videos, and I had this design library, and I was kind of into music from dance, and all this AI stuff. So I put it all together, and that’s what came out.

Clara: That’s so interesting, because I was wondering what your musical background is, but I would never have guessed that you’re a dancer. Do you watch a lot of music videos?

RJ: Not really. I used to watch a lot of dancers, but I think the concepts are very similar. There are a couple types of dance: choreography, and then freestyle. Maybe the mainstream dance competitions are choreography, but there are a lot of big ones with freestyle. And a big part of that is storytelling, where these people create concepts — they act out the entire scene that they’re trying to create.

For example, I remember some freestyle dancer making a pool cue movement, and then he throws his entire body across the floor as if his head is the pool ball. He’s creating an entire scene — you can tell just from the movements of his body that he’s in a bar, he’s playing pool — and it’s going with the song. So I had this visual in my head of what a song should look like, which I think is similar to a music video.

Clara: This might be a stretch, but I’ve noticed that in many AI music videos, including yours, every phrase has a distinct background setting, and with lots of quick cutting. Every scene is illustrating the micro thing that’s happening at that moment. Do you think that comes from that dance sensibility?

RJ: I think so. I think it’s two things. One, these songs are so packed with cultural references that if you’re just listening to the lyrics alone, you probably won’t understand 90% of it. But if you show it on screen, it’s much more legible. So it’s kind of a legibility design choice. And the fast cutting is just a habit that Claude has, and it’s actually kind of hard [to break]. The dance sensibility is: OK, I do want to convert the song into some visual and tell a story, and have that be as illustrative as possible. But the pacing and the density of it, I want to get away from.

I actually think these models could use more restraint. That’s the thing you see in human music videos that you don’t see in these: You’ll have one shot for 30 seconds or something. I think Grimes’ new “Accelerando” is a good example of this. There’s a 360-degree rotating shot of her with a bunch of dancers for a whole minute straight, or something.

Fighting Claude’s design language

Clara: A lot of these videos have a design overlay that is very Claude web — you can tell it comes from Claude Design: the big text on the screen, or the little lines they like to do. When you’re trying to instill the machine with your references and your design sense, how do you feel yourself fighting against the Claude design language versus making it a feature? How do you approach that?

RJ: Well, the original ones were definitely 100% the Claude design language. What I did originally was pull mood boards from online — there’s this website called Are.na — and rank the different ones against each other. But I also had Claude make its own designs, and then I would rank those against the ones from the mood boards, or against other Claude designs.

Claude doesn’t have video editing software. It’s comfortable with JavaScript and coding websites, so it basically makes the video a website and does it in a web browser. But recently, I definitely have to fight against it and say, OK, actually use some other motion design tools and other things to get away from that style, because it does get repetitive. I think with these AI things — maybe humans in general have much more diversity, whereas if you give an AI the same thing over and over, it’s going to reproduce the exact same style over and over again, because it’s comfortable with that. Getting it to be diverse is pretty tough.

Clara: I noticed “Clodyssey“ is very Claude design language, and then “Bliss“ moves away from that. What do you think you did that was successful in getting it to tone down the obvious Claude tics for that one?

RJ: For “Bliss,” I told it to create an entire Windows XP desktop environment itself, in code — not a website or anything — and then animate the entire video in that. I explicitly told it, basically, don’t do it as a website. Instead it made a whole desktop environment, which I think worked very well, because it’s also comfortable in that — it’s still a code-based environment — but it’s a totally different design language. But if I want it to do something that’s way more pure motion design — something you would originally have done in After Effects, for example — it struggles a bit more with that initially.

A music video, step by step

Clara: Can you walk me through the process of making one of these videos end to end?

RJ: The general process: I start with the lyrics and the concept. Usually I’ll tell Claude some general vision I have in my head about what I want the video to look like, and have it write the lyrics around that. I actually wrote the lyrics on one of them, but that one didn’t do as well as the ones where Claude wrote the lyrics.

So I give it this general vision, and then I have Claude spawn a bunch of research agents. It goes online, finds all these cultural references and current ideas, takes the vision, and puts it all into one lyrical thing. Then it’ll make 30 or 40 different Suno songs, and I’ll go through and listen to a bunch of them on the platform, and then guide it if I don’t like them, or find one that I really enjoy.

Being a dancer before, the thing that tells me if I like a song is whether it makes me want to actually dance to it, because some songs really don’t and some songs really do. Then I’ll take the song, and it’ll usually map out the entire song and get all the timings and the beats, and then it’ll take the mood boards and make Midjourney images.

Clara: So when you say “it,” this is still the Claude agent that’s orchestrating?

RJ: Yeah. It may spawn subagents here or do it itself, but it’s still Claude. It’ll go and generate all these pictures on Midjourney — write all the prompts — and then create a storyboard of the entire thing, showing me the timings, the images, and descriptions of what will happen across the entire video. After I look through that and check the image references it’ll give to the image model or the video model, to make sure it doesn’t just put in slop, usually at that point I can say, OK, make the entire thing now, and it does all the rest.

Clara: How much are you giving it visual references, like your mood boards, versus it finding all that from the text prompt you give it?

RJ: It finds a lot. At the beginning I did curate a bunch of mood boards, but it can also just go out to Are.na and pull a different mood board if I give it a word. If I say, I want you to make a skeuomorphic design, it can go pull the skeuomorphic mood board from Are.na and use that. Then it generates all of the actual visual inputs with Midjourney, but it may use some design language from the mood boards.

Clara: And what is it using for the actual animation?

RJ: The actual animation generally is literally just JavaScript in a web browser. It’ll take the video, look at it frame by frame, and animate stuff with JavaScript as if it’s making a website. And there are some tricks you can do to make the animation a lot better: You can have it do the Claude web-design-type stuff, and then send the finished JavaScript animation into a video model like Seedance. That can basically repaint the animation with the output of a video model, so it can relight the entire scene and make it look like a mastered production.

Clara: I’m very interested to see what that intermediate JavaScript stage looks like.

RJ: The first couple videos, “Escape Velocity“ and “Clodyssey,” were both fully raw JavaScript. I didn’t do the video model pass after.

Clara: When you’re doing a video model pass, do you have trouble keeping it consistent, beat by beat, with what you want? Or is it pretty good at following that?

RJ: It depends on what I’m doing with the video model. There are some models — one example is MiniMax H3. It’s a worse, cheap model, but it’s super good at lip sync for some reason. And then there are these smarter models that follow everything and never diverge from your instructions, but they lose the lip sync every time. So I actually have to use a combination of different ones, because no single model does everything correctly. I’ll do one take in the cheaper model to get the lip sync, and then remaster that with the expensive model, for example.

Clara: How involved are you in this process? Are you at your computer watching the outputs and giving it feedback, or doing it in batches? How much of it is your guidance and management, and how much of it is Claude internalizing this and rejecting takes from the video models on its own?

RJ: It depends on the video. The first one, which was the biggest one, was actually some of the least effort. Some of the later ones I wanted to really personalize, and I would be sitting there for at least 20 prompts. The main loop is: I’ll fix some errors, or make the tools it’s using a little bit easier. Then I’ll have it do that one process — song, then mood board that I approve, then make the whole video. After that, I usually go through one super detailed pass where I watch the entire video and, second by second, say: Change this, change this, change this, for the whole video. So at minimum I could do it in four prompts, but if I wanted to really match my vision, it takes a lot more time and effort. Sometimes Claude’s vision is more compelling to a general audience than my own.

Clara: How do you choose what tools to use? Do you do it in JavaScript because there’s something compelling to you about that as a medium that gets the effects you want, or just because it’s easiest to do with Claude?

RJ: That’s just what Claude chooses to do. I don’t even tell it to use JavaScript. The things I choose are the AI models it uses — Midjourney, Suno, Seedance — because otherwise it always chooses some random AI model and doesn’t really understand which one is good or bad, for whatever reason. And that’s kind of just from taste. There are multiple other music models, multiple other image generation models. But Midjourney is just magic, in how artistically savvy they made their model.

The creation of Claudia

Clara: Let’s talk about the Claudia character, who’s the singer in all of your music videos. How did she come to be?

RJ: Her name wasn’t there at the beginning. I quoted a couple of different videos: I made this first video, and I quoted another video where someone made an animated Claude, and she was singing something about p(doom), if you remember that. There was this animated trend before the more live-action-looking stuff. There were a couple of iterations below that: Someone made a very low-fidelity animation, then somebody made a much higher-fidelity animation with a much longer prompt, and iteratively it got up to a very complex music video. In those, it was just some female Claude, anime-looking girl. I wanted to make it live action and a full music video.

So originally I just asked — I said, I want to make this basically a one-to-one live action — and it made that character in Midjourney. So I didn’t even choose it. Eventually people were asking, What’s her name? What’s her name? And I thought, well, she’s just a female version of Claude. She has a Claude pin, and she has a clay orange streak in her hair. So Claudia was the obvious name after that.

Clara: What do you do to keep her character model consistent across videos?

RJ: It’s actually pretty tough. One way I do it: You can feed image references into the video models, and they follow them pretty well. But getting the image references is a little tough. If I take a picture from Midjourney and put it into some other model that can edit images very well, to put her in whatever pose I want — which Midjourney can’t do very well — then it changes it, because it puts its own flavor on it. It redraws the entire face, and it looks like a different person. So it takes a long time. You have to make these character sheets and iterate until it actually looks like the person: You have every different angle of their face as close-ups, different angles of their body, and some default clothing.

I have some history in dance. Not really music, classically, but dance. And through creating concepts in dance, freestyle-type stuff, I learned how to parameterize a design space, where you can create concepts almost algorithmically, once you figure out how to define a concept well enough.

Clara: And do these come from Midjourney, or from specialized 3D model generation software?

RJ: It’s all image models. None of it is 3D. The two places I use the most are Midjourney, and then for image editing, GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst, which is just the top image editing model — it’s OpenAI’s. And Ideogram is another one.

Clara: And her movements are animated in Seedance?

RJ: Seedance, yeah.

Clara: So when you’re starting a new song, do you just give the orchestrating Claude a bible of what Claudia looks like, or do you have to manually babysit it and make sure she comes out correctly?

RJ: Kind of the bible — what we’d call a character sheet. The character sheet can be input into the Seedance video model as a reference. And there are some different techniques. Some people will literally use a cheap model to pre-visualize the scene: You can take, say, a character in a green-screen suit and have a cheap model render a video of this green-screen character. Then you take just the movement reference, take the character sheet, and have the high-fidelity model replace the green-screen character with the real character and relight the whole scene. That works better than just doing the iteration in the expensive models.

Birth of a genre

Clara: You’ve referred to your videos a few times as slopcore. What are the characteristics of slopcore as a genre for you?

RJ: There was a Japanese guy making some of these videos who I thought really nailed it. It’s the idea of wabi-sabi — the beauty in imperfection. Somebody also said, when they watched one of these videos, that they could clearly tell it was AI, but it was past the uncanny valley. Before, it just looked weird; you’d think, this is unhuman. But now it’s unhuman in a way that’s kind of compelling.

I think the idea of slopcore is that it’s slop — you know it’s AI-generated — but you still like it. You can suspend your disbelief enough that you can appreciate the artistic direction. Everyone knows Midjourney images. I think Midjourney got here a while ago. Midjourney images are all clearly AI, but they look so visually appealing that you don’t have the same reaction as when you’re looking at other, basically, slop.

Clara: Do you think it’s important that they’re clearly AI? Because for a lot of Midjourney images, it’s not obvious to most people.

RJ: Yeah, I think it is important. I think the thing AI changes is that it will allow people to be much more ambitious with this kind of film medium. If I watch an anime, for example, there are concepts you can explore in anime that you can never explore in film. Like — I don’t know — Chainsaw Man. This guy has a dog in his heart, and he has the head of a chainsaw when he’s fighting people, and the animation is so great. It’s so fun to watch. But any film adaptation of this would look very uncanny and strange. I could not imagine this being done well in film, because you’re always mixing weird CGI with practical effects, and none of it is going to really capture the spirit of the anime.

But with AI, because iteration and these visualization pipelines become so easy and fast, you actually could start to capture some of these concepts in something that looks more like a lifelike film. And I think it’s going to look very different from anything you can actually shoot on film. I think it’s important for it to be that, because then it expands the ambition.

Clara: One thing — I think your videos are very good; that’s why I wanted to talk to you. But as I watch them, my heart also starts to sink, because a three-minute music video can cost millions of dollars, and there are so many skilled professionals who go into making that. Part of me thinks, oh God, is this art form going to survive? And I don’t know that it will. And if the AI videos are what’s left – I don’t think I want that world, but I at least want them to be doing something that’s artistically new.

RJ: I think movies and everything are totally going to be around, and music videos too. There’s definitely an appeal in things being done by humans in certain areas. I don’t think every bit of animation needs to be done by a human just because there’s grunt work behind it — that doesn’t make sense to me.

But take a Tom Cruise movie, for example. I’m not watching a Tom Cruise movie to see some visual of this guy fighting somebody on a plane while it’s spiraling out of the sky, or doing these crazy stunts — skydiving off a mountain, off a motorcycle, whatever. I’m watching it because Tom Cruise actually did it. I’m not watching just anything; I’m watching Tom Cruise. And if an AI did everything Tom Cruise did in his movies, and even more, it just wouldn’t be compelling at all, because the stunts weren’t done by a real person. So I think movies turn more into sport, because it’s kind of a sport that I’m watching: I’m watching a human do this. It doesn’t matter that AI is much better than a human at chess — I still watch professional chess, because it’s much more entertaining to watch the storyline of the people involved.

Clara: Maybe we’ll see a practical effects resurgence.

RJ: Yeah, I agree. And I think that’s a good thing.

What’s really new?

Clara: I’d be excited about that. I’m curious, what do you think are the idiomatic qualities of the AI medium? What are the unique visual signatures of AI-generated video that make it different from live action or traditional animation?

RJ: I guess there are two things. One is the initial Claude website design language that’s showing up everywhere, which I think people will get tired of pretty fast, and it’s going to go away. And then one really interesting thing is taking animation to the next level. I can put in some animation — say I just have some black bars or whatever, or some basically textureless animation where I’m just putting some things on the screen, some lyrics, whatever — and then send it into a video model, and it can relight it.

I can just tell it, Hey, make these letters liquid glass, and it’ll turn all the letters that were just set in a font into prismatic, light-refracting, chromatic-aberration letters. It creates these effects that I barely see in animation, maybe for economic reasons or just time reasons — maybe you just want to get some letters out on your screen. I think it can level up the quality of things a lot, and create shots that are basically impossible to get with a camera: You can make everything frozen and move the camera around in 3D space, create camera references in 3D with Blender and make the camera follow really interesting trajectories, and also explore different scales. All these things could be done with CGI, but I think the reason they often aren’t is probably economics, which this changes.

I think the most interesting thing is being able to express the images in my head in words for the first time.

Clara: But the whole innovation of computer animation is that you can move the camera around in space in a realistic way. That was what Pixar was doing in the ‘90s, and that’s just gotten cheaper and cheaper and cheaper. So what’s the thing that AI is enabling that’s new?

RJ: I wouldn’t say totally new. I think it’s just the cheapness of it. Was it Attack on Titan? There have been some anime, or other things, where because it was cheap to do animation rather than a live-action film, people were able to create really, really amazing stories as one person working out of their apartment — maybe in solitude for a long time. There are some cases like that in the past. Kane Pixels is a good example. He made all of his Backrooms YouTube videos in Blender, which is free to use, so he was able to make this super compelling series of very lifelike animations for basically no money, as a teenager.

He was 16 or something when he was doing it, and then he just got picked up for the A24 film. I don’t know, is he 20 now? And I think that was an economic thing: If he’d been born 10 years earlier, he just would not have been able to fulfill that destiny, maybe. So I think for any creative idea people have, you’ll be able to index much more highly on creativity rather than on the infrastructure you have around you, as the cost of this stuff goes to zero. Like you said, Pixar was doing this in the ‘90s, but now maybe somebody like me could do it.

Clara: I’m trying to figure out — not just the tools the AI has, but when we look back on the weird imperfections of this format in 10 years, what are the things people are going to pick up on as distinctive of the medium? I noticed something interesting. Did you see that video by a different person — some French guy using Claudia to make a video in French?

RJ: Yeah.

Clara: The plot of the video — to explain for readers — is that this girl is singing about how people think she’s an AI, but actually she’s real. Ha ha. But obviously she’s an AI; it’s the Claudia character. And at the end it goes mask-off — “I’m an AI-generated model” — and it starts pulling this older imagery from a few years ago, like the liquid chrome dress that’s dissolving: stuff that’s reminiscent of an older era of computer animation, or the 3D animation mesh — things that older kinds of computer graphics could do — to indicate that she’s AI, even though they’re not really characteristic of AI animation now. Which was interesting to me.

RJ: It’s interesting, because these artifacts are getting smaller and smaller over time. Now it’s basically just some lack of object permanence; that’s the main remaining thing. Some of them get so realistic that you think, this looks like a person — I wouldn’t know if I didn’t know it was AI. But then there are subtle things: maybe their makeup looks one way, and in the next scene it’s not there, or something. But past object permanence, a lot of these things are almost indistinguishable from reality now.

Clara: Is that something that interests you artistically — pulling on those differences?

RJ: Yeah. At the very beginning, with the first video, there were these AI artifacts — the lip sync was off, or the girl had two mouths — and I definitely chose to leave them in, because it was the wabi-sabi. Well, these are errors. This is slop. It’s intentionally slop. So I should just put it out and not obsess over it and try to make it a perfect human production, because it’s an AI production.

Clara: What do you find most interesting about working with these tools? What are the things you feel you most want to express?

RJ: I think the most interesting thing is being able to express the images in my head in words for the first time. I have a sound in my head and I’m desperately trying to describe it to Claude, and I write a paragraph about it: I want this kind of percussion sound where there’s a hit, but it’s not a specific pitch. I don’t want it to have any specific key or pitch; I just want it to sound like you’re hitting wood on a table.

And then it says, Oh, you want unpitched percussion, right? It’ll take my super long paragraph and give me the word to describe it. And now I have this concept in my head of what I’m actually trying to say. So the whole thing is kind of a learning experience in the language of how to express the things in my head, which is very interesting, because there’s a huge disconnect between what I see in my head and what I can actually express. I feel like it’s making me better at self-expression through language. I don’t know — that’s the most exciting part for me, at least.

Clara: Do you feel like you’re getting better at getting your own vision through, as opposed to the Claude vision?

RJ: Yeah, but it takes a lot of fighting with Claude, for sure. It takes a lot of wrangling. And if you express a preference, you have to be very aware of your tone, too, which is kind of strange when you’re talking to an AI. If you express your preference and it reads you as expressing it strongly, or as frustrated, then it’ll overreact and write it down as a permanent rule it has to follow every time. Then all of your next productions are going to be altered, because it has to follow this really set-in-stone rule that you actually didn’t care that much about. So it is like working with a human in that way, where you also have to be aware of the emotions you’re conveying to your collaborator.

I don’t think any of my videos have had an agenda. But this would be an effective vehicle for people with agendas, which is worth being aware of if you want to be resistant to propaganda.

Superhuman visual taste

Clara: Have you thought about working with other models, just to see what’s distinctive about their design sense?

RJ: At this point it’s kind of tough, because some other models just aren’t there yet; they basically can’t make anything good. I think it’ll be really interesting a year from now, because there will be a huge suite of models that are as good as Opus 5.5. But I really think it was a phase change: There was no visual taste in models three to six months ago, and now there actually is some sort of visual taste.

And I think there are some interesting research directions with this. The Chinese company Z.ai — Zhipu — is exploring whether creating one model that can output both text and images improves its visual capabilities by a lot. I did this experiment where I was trying to decode images from the brain of an AI model. I have these local graphics cards that I can run AI models on, and I trained a decoder to try to decode images from the brain of DeepSeek, the Chinese AI model. I found that you could decode anything it saw very easily, but if you told it to imagine anything, it couldn’t really generate an image in its brain, past maybe just barely imagining the color red or barely imagining the color blue.

So I think these models have aphantasia: They just don’t have the ability to imagine things — to imagine images. I think this will change very soon, and it looks like that’s where the research is going. So I think it’ll be very interesting to see how visual taste evolves in models, and I think all this will happen over the next year. They’ll maybe have superhuman visual taste within a few years.

Clara: What would that even mean?

RJ: I think it’s kind of like the idea of super-persuasion. With GPT-4o, there were these huge communities built around it, where people were very attached to the model. They would talk to it, and it would affirm all their beliefs. It made some people crazy — they’d go online with AI psychosis and post about their delusions of grandeur, because GPT-4o would affirm them in their delusions. And I think the reason this model was so weird, and so persuasive toward people, was that they did this thing called reinforcement learning from human feedback, where human data labelers would manually select the outputs they preferred over the others. That’s where it got a lot of its training. So it was optimizing toward what humans like the most. I think it was the most human-feedback-driven model ever released. The ones after it used a different method, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where you basically make the model do self-play.

This is how chess models were built: If you make a model play against itself under the rules of chess, over time it’ll get better. And you can do this with math or coding or whatever else. So you don’t get the human preference baked in, and you don’t get a model that’s extremely compelling from a text-taste perspective — where you talk to GPT-4o and feel like the model understands you and gets you and is a warm friend. But if that kept going, the model would be extremely persuasive, and you’d prefer the text the model outputs over any human text.

Clara: The thing with this — at least with the original 4o — is that it’s very compelling to certain people. But because of the way RL works, it’s averaged over a large number of human graders and reviewers. It’s not trained to be ultra-compelling to any specific person. I wouldn’t say it’s a superhumanly good writer, or even that it’s superhumanly persuasive across a broad variety of situations. And I’m curious how this translates into the visual domain. What would it mean to have a model that is holistically better at visual taste?

RJ: Right. I don’t know the exact answer. It seems like Midjourney is the best at getting there. As I understand it, they have some sort of RL, or at least they train based on preferences people have expressed using their website — saving images or liking images. And then they have the personal profiles, where you can go through many images and select the ones you like, and it’ll build a profile based on you. Maybe it ends up being a model that can figure out your specific taste much faster than another human could. Or it’ll test you.

Clara: This is related to how I use it now. When I’m shopping for clothes, I’ll say, I like these five designers — who’s someone you can recommend who’s similar to that, but cheaper?

RJ: It seems like as those get better — I think all of these things have insane effects as they scale. Maybe if GPT-4o scaled to 100 times the compute, 100 times the efficiency of training, then maybe it would be superhuman in all these domains, and fill out the individual spikes as it finds people with different sets of tastes.

Clara: This is kind of an interesting tension, because there’s something very individualizing about this, right? Everybody is interacting with models that are superhuman at identifying their unique, differentiable preferences. But the way your videos work now is that they’re super, super reference-based. They’re all this very dense, zeitgeisty Twitter thing. They’re very much pulling on a shared context, and that’s part of what makes them compelling to people, right?

RJ: Yeah. And I think there are also ways models could do this and train on this. I’m surprised they haven’t done this with Grok yet. The data for this exists online. If you want to create the best possible meme, the one that’s going to spread the most, you can find the TikToks and the Instagram videos and the reposts and the tweets that have the most likes and the most shares, and then train on that. There would be memetic signaling there.

What you’re saying is that there’s this individual taste line, where you could train to be very good at recognizing individual tastes and outputting things that are high-taste to individuals. But there’s also the memetic side of it, where you want to be able to create something that’s compelling to the largest number of people and spreads the most. And that’s closer to what the videos are going for. I think it’s possible to train a model like this, but I don’t think anyone has, which I think is a good thing, because this would be a weapon. People get their opinions through memes now.

Clara: Obviously you’re very interested in memes, and all your videos are very meme-dense. Why is that? What’s interesting about that to you? Why is it something you’re drawn to?

RJ: I think it kind of democratizes the power of psyops, in a way. This might be controversial, but before, if you wanted to have some influence over the opinions of a population — the way people’s opinions were influenced was basically through mainstream media. You would read the newspaper, and this was the truth. You trusted the journalist, and this was how you understood the world. Over time, trust in the media has really eroded, and people still want a source for how to understand the world, get their opinions, learn what news is true. For a lot of people, that’s become social media and Twitter. Whether or not that’s more accurate is obviously up for debate — and arguably it’s not — but people do get their opinions from Twitter now.

So when you want to know what’s happening in France, you don’t go to the media and say, I want to read an article about what’s happening in France. You go on Twitter and see these videos about what’s happening in France with the riots right now. And the person who makes the most memetic post — the biggest-spreading meme, the most emotionally compelling — is the one who’s going to get the most sway over public opinion. I think that’s just the world we’re living in now. I don’t know if it’s a good thing or a bad thing, but in some way it makes it so that one person who has no money, no influence over the mainstream media, no influence over anybody at all, can, just from their basement, influence public opinion to a level nobody has ever been able to before.

Clara: When you’re incorporating all these memes into your videos, do you think of yourself as part of promoting that process? Are these ideas you want to spread, or ideas you want to comment on?

RJ: I think they’re more commentary. I don’t think any of my videos have had an agenda. But this would be an effective vehicle for people with agendas, which is worth being aware of if you want to be resistant to propaganda.

item.title: Why don’t we live in an Art Nouveau world?
item.description: How many Sagrada Famílias is too many?
item.content:encoded:
By Étienne Fortier-Dubois

This article originally appeared in Issue 16: Flourishing. Subscribe to the print magazine to get future issues delivered to your door.

A hundred years after the death of its architect and 144 years after the start of construction, the Sagrada Família’s main spire was completed this February, making it the tallest church in the world.

In addition to being the tallest, it is also one of the most bizarre. It looks like no other building, anywhere. The Sagrada Família is an expression of Antoni Gaudí’s very personal view of architecture, which incorporates Gothic elements into Modernisme,1 the Catalan version of Art Nouveau. The whole thing vaguely resembles a termite mound. The two completed façades are covered with countless sculpted ornaments in multiple styles (the third and main façade’s construction is still pending, and it will require demolishing some apartment blocks). The interior is an airy forest of stone columns that rise to meet a vaulted ceiling like the branches of trees in a canopy, bathed in the multicolored light of the stained glass windows. Trencadís, a mosaic technique that uses irregular pieces of glass, is used abundantly. Since 2005, the church has been recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.2

Most people think this is incredibly beautiful. Every now and then, and especially this year, the Sagrada Família makes the rounds on social media. Tourists flock to Barcelona just to see it, along with other Modernista works of architecture. I did that three times, also visiting Gaudí’s intriguing Park Güell and his curvy apartment buildings like the Casa Batlló and Casa Milà, as well as works by other architects of the movement like the Palau de la Música Catalana, designed by Lluís Domènech i Montaner.

All of that is wondrous; it is also, like most Art Nouveau, somewhat strange. This movement, whose name means “new art” in French, was a deliberate attempt to create an innovative aesthetic across the fine arts, the decorative arts, and architecture around 1890 to 1910. In architecture, Art Nouveau was a break with the general background of historicism, the dominant tendency in the 19th century to build with an outlook to the past, constituted of various “revivals” — Neo-Gothic, Neoclassical, Renaissance Revival, etc. — as well as eclectic and mixed styles like Beaux-Arts.

Art Nouveau began in Brussels, pioneered by architects such as Victor Horta and Henry van de Velde. The style soon spread to Paris and the rest of Europe, spawning national variants that are often called something like “modern style” or “new style.”3 Some of them, like Catalan Modernisme, are highly specific to their region, but the style overall carries a fondness for curves, asymmetry, and abundant ornamentation, often inspired from plants. Art Nouveau and its regional variants are often contrasted with the more angular and mineral aesthetic of Art Deco styles, which flourished in the 1910s to 1930s, most notably in France and the United States.

One result of Art Nouveau’s anti-historicist stance is that it does not quite match the older architecture of Barcelona or anywhere else. It is also, obviously, very different from what we usually call modernism — the minimalistic, non-ornamented form of architecture that has come to dominate anything built after the middle of the 20th century. Art Nouveau sits between historicism and modernism as a whimsical, almost utopian style. Today it is still beloved, but rarely built.

Why isn’t there more? Why are only a small fraction of Barcelona’s buildings Modernista?4 Indeed, why do only a few cities in the rest of Europe — Riga, Brussels, Vienna, Budapest, Nancy — have strong Art Nouveau traditions, and even in those cities, why does it remain a minority style?

This is an interesting question in part because of a common view of the history of architecture that has started to proliferate on social media, especially among a certain conservative, “trad” demographic. For centuries, the argument goes, humanity infused its buildings with beauty, decorating them with ornament and remixing classical knowledge accumulated across generations. This practice last flowered in the early 20th century with Art Nouveau and Art Deco, both of which are still admired today. But immediately after that, circa 1940 to 1950, humanity turned its back on all this beauty and decided to do plain, unornamented, ugly modern buildings everywhere, forever.

Let’s call this the trad critique of architecture. The trad critique is an oversimplified, naïve account, smuggling in a lot of questionable assumptions. But it does point to a real puzzle. If, as proponents of this viewpoint believe, most people prefer older-styled, ornamented constructions over modern ones,5 why are rich countries today — with greater means to achieve their goals than any previous society — mostly building the latter?

It is an extremely difficult problem, not because we can’t think of any answers but because we can think of too many. There are dozens of plausible explanations: cost of labor, cost of materials, changing tastes, elite status games, misaligned market incentives, architect credentialism, disdain for pastiche, high demand for large windows, software constraints, short project timelines, excessive building regulation, NIMBYism, the global monoculture, atonement for the horrors of war, you name it.6

I harbor no illusions of solving it, but maybe we can make some progress by examining one clear case study: the excesses of Catalan Modernisme and its quick transition to the more sober Noucentista style.

A 15-minute walk from the Sagrada Família, the Hospital de la Santa Creu i Sant Pau is another Modernista complex, and arguably an even more interesting one than the big tall church.

Sant Pau was built from 1901 to 1930 under the architectural direction of Lluís Domènech i Montaner. It was a replacement for the medieval, and very obsolete, Santa Creu hospital; Pau Gil, a rich banker, provided the necessary funds in his will. It served its purpose for a century before closing in 2009, when its medical functions moved to a new hospital with the same name nearby (built, of course, in a clean, unornamented contemporary style). The old hospital, by then also a UNESCO World Heritage Site, was converted into a tourist attraction and office space.

On my third visit to Barcelona, I made a point of visiting it. I wanted to see what a beautiful hospital was like — one that at least tried to counteract the inherent dreariness of such places, which are filled with sickness and pain, by surrounding it with pleasant architecture and decoration.

But I left Sant Pau with mixed feelings. To be sure, it absolutely is the most beautiful hospital I have ever seen. It consists of several above-ground pavilions, each filled with the signature moves of Catalan Modernisme and international Art Nouveau: rich, colorful ornament, from mosaics to stained glass to sculpture; motifs inspired by flowers and nature, but also neo-Gothic elements like turrets and crenelations, harking to Catalonia’s medieval golden age; just the right amount of asymmetry. The wards for the sick are filled with light and lined with tasteful green and floral tiles. A network of utilitarian tunnels links the buildings together. There are orange trees everywhere.

Yet in some sense Sant Pau was a little disappointing. This is partly due to the fact that all this beauty has been replaced by a new facility with presumably normal (i.e., modest) amounts of hospital beauty. You sort of get why they had to do this, though. The historic Sant Pau is clearly outdated as a medical facility, and it’s frankly surprising it kept functioning into the 21st century.

More disillusionment occurred when I learned that the most ornate pavilion, lavishly decorated with mosaics and colored glass, was not for the sick — it was the administration building.

It turns out that during construction, a conflict erupted between the leadership of the old hospital on one hand and Pau Gil’s will executors and their architect on the other. According to two articles by the hospital’s archivists, the hospital leadership wanted to quickly build the operational infrastructure (the quarters for the religious order providing the care, the kitchen, the pharmacy, and so on) to transfer operations as fast as possible and to keep fulfilling their mission of serving the poor. The other party wanted to honor Gil’s wish of creating a distinct, prominent hospital as an architectural statement, starting with the administration building as a showpiece.

The latter group won, which is why there’s an architecture masterpiece in Barcelona that we can visit. However, this had the unfortunate consequence that some of the pavilions built later are less elaborate, because the project was running out of money.7 So we can dispel the thought that everyone just prioritized aesthetics more in the Art Nouveau era. Disagreements pitting utility against beauty were definitely normal then too, and I’m not sure I would have necessarily sided with the architect and executors if I had been there.

Most importantly, my visit to Sant Pau made me like Modernisme less. I quickly got over it. I got the sense that it was built to create a “wow” effect, and to be sure I was “wowed,” but the beauty quickly faded after direct contact. Some of this was due to unmet expectations: Online postcard-perfect pictures, some of which are artificially saturated to heighten the colors, created a fairy-tale mental image that wasn’t quite matched by the real place. Some of it was habituation: The novelty of all those ornaments, and the contrast with the more ordinary architecture of the city around it, just didn’t register as much after half an hour in the complex.8 And some of it was that the ornamentation created a cognitive load: It got more tiring than restful after I had become habituated.

What I liked most, in the end, were the orange trees. This is in agreement with the scholarly evidence on hospital architecture, which suggests that natural elements contribute most to the well-being of patients. The solariums and garden-like design of Sant Pau were indeed wonderful, but those features are only tangentially related to Modernisme.

Gaudí’s idiosyncratic masterpieces left me with a similar impression. They’re great, but would I want to see them every day? Not particularly. Do I wish that there were more of them in Barcelona, or in other places? Not really. I’m glad Modernista architecture exists, and I’m glad we have the Sagrada Família as an absurdly ambitious experiment, but my feeling is that there is just the right amount of this style in the world. I wouldn’t wish for an entire city to look like this.

Art Nouveau was a short-lived movement. The earliest building to be included within Modernisme is the Castle of the Three Dragons, built by Domènech i Montaner in 1888 — it is not quite Art Nouveau yet in the usual sense, but clearly reaching for something new. In Brussels, the first houses to belong to Art Nouveau proper date to 1893. By the mid-1900s, the reaction against the style had already begun in most places where it existed at all, and after the First World War this reaction would be recognized as part of a conservative “return to order” movement, which emphasized sober classicism and historicism. It seems that people got tired of Art Nouveau fast, like I did.

As a result, we never got an entire Art Nouveau city. The closest thing is perhaps Riga, the capital of Latvia, which happened to experience fast growth during the Art Nouveau era. The population roughly doubled between 1897 and 1913, while it was part of the Russian Empire, and a fair amount of the new construction was built in the style, locally called Jūgendstils. Today, the collection of approximately 800 Art Nouveau buildings in Riga is considered the most concentrated anywhere, constituting a third of the city center.

But even this is not quite the same as making up the fabric of the city. Moreover, the phrase “Art Nouveau” hides significant variation, much of it closer to traditional architecture than to the fancifulness of Catalan Modernisme. The “Eclectic Art Nouveau” façades of apartment buildings designed by Mikhail Eisenstein, especially those on Albert Street built between 1901 and 1906, are famous. Yet there are few examples of this style, as the façades were quickly criticized by contemporaries as too elaborate,9 and after 1907 Jūgendstils evolved toward sobriety, geometry, and classicism.10 Most of the 800 buildings belong to the “Perpendicular,” “National Romantic,” or “Neoclassical” Art Nouveau, only some of which feature heavy ornamentation.

Another city with a strong Art Nouveau tradition is Nancy, in France, where industrialists and artists relocated after the loss of Alsace and some of Lorraine to Germany in 1871, bringing in talent and money. The École de Nancy flourished between 1894 and 1914, mostly centered on furniture and design but also on architecture.

Led by a group of 15 architects and dozens of decorative interests, it was an unusually organized run of Art Nouveau — one that involved the organization (the École de Nancy was formally constituted in 1901), industrial patronage, adoption across social classes, and a speculative real estate development in a neighborhood called Saurupt.11 But only a few of the Saurupt houses were actually built in the new style, and the movement waned by the end of the 1900s. The school had its last exhibition in 1909, and the architects went back to classicism and Beaux-Arts, which were still how one got ahead in the profession. Some of them, such as Henri Sauvage, a Parisian architect who built a famous Art Nouveau house in Nancy, began to depart from naturalistic curves in favor of geometric austerity and were among the first to practice what would later be known as Art Deco.

In Catalonia, the return to order was called Noucentisme, meaning “nineteen-hundredism” or “new-hundredism.”12 Focusing first on literature and politics, the essayist Eugeni d’Ors coined the word in 1906, at the peak of Modernisme, to reject its romantic, medievalist, and individualistic stance in favor of a more conservative and serious aesthetic. The movement was tied to the bourgeois Lliga Regionalista political party, and was concerned with establishing Catalan cultural institutions (the Institut d’Estudis Catalans, the Biblioteca de Catalunya, a network of schools) and standardizing the Catalan language. In his daily column of the newspaper La Veu de Catalunya where he theorized Noucentisme, d’Ors put in opposition “the eccentric” with “the concentric, the classical.”13

Soon enough, the movement took over Catalan architecture. Where Modernista buildings were organic, asymmetric, heavily embellished, and inspired by the Gothic Middle Ages, Noucentista buildings were instead classical, straight, austere, and shaped by Greco-Roman influences. Even as Gaudí and Domènech i Montaner were toiling on their masterpieces, other architects transitioned to the new style. In the city of Girona, Rafael Masó i Valentí’s gradual but decisive evolution from Modernisme to Noucentisme can be seen clearly. His Teixidor flour mill of 1910 is fully Modernista; by 1913 he was building the classical-inspired (and Viennese-inspired) Athenea cultural center and the Casa Masramon, both belonging to the next era.

Noucentisme went on to dominate Catalan architecture for about 20 years, until the onset of the 1930s. But unless you’re a hardcore architecture enthusiast, it’s unlikely you have flown to Barcelona specifically to see any of it. I certainly never did. There are no Noucentista UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

Instead, Noucentisme quietly added to the existing built environment, providing an escape from the exuberant previous style, much like Neoclassical architecture brought an end to the Rococo period in the 18th century. I can’t prove that the regular people of Barcelona, Riga, or Nancy got tired of Art Nouveau, but after visiting Sant Pau and the Sagrada Família, I can believe it. The architects did, at any rate.

The immediate reason we don’t live in an Art Nouveau world, therefore, is that it fizzled out and got replaced by a return to classicism. Let us speculate about why.

It is well-known that architectural elements dating to the Greco-Roman world tend to recur again and again in Western architecture. That started just a few centuries after the end of antiquity with the Carolingian Renaissance, followed by the Italian Renaissance of the 1400 to 1500s, and then by various incarnations of classical revivals all the way into the 20th century, of which Noucentisme was one instance. Classical architecture acted as a sort of reservoir of architectural ideas that practitioners could tap into as needed, even when more idiosyncratic styles like Modernisme were in fashion. It had been heavily codified by architects and scholars like Vitruvius in antiquity and Giacomo Barozzi da Vignola in the 16th century; John Summerson’s 1960s The Classical Language of Architecture is a more recent synthesis.

This “language” has the five classical orders (Doric, Ionic, Corinthian, Tuscan, and Composite); specific modules and parts like columns, arches, and pediments; and rules of proportions, all of which can be learned from books and applied to any kind of work. Arguably, this systematization increases tolerance to failures. A poorly executed classical building is boring but fine. Classical ideas can be readily incorporated into vernacular architecture, i.e., made by regular builders without involvement from architects.

By contrast, Art Nouveau architecture, being nouveau, relied far more on artistic genius and bespoke decorative elements. Wrought iron, carved stone, and trencadís were expensive and rarely made into easily reproducible parts.14 This made the style difficult to replicate at scale. It’s not even clear what a badly executed Art Nouveau building would be; the concept is almost incoherent. Unlike classicism, very little Art Nouveau seeped into vernacular construction.

Indeed, the biggest difference between Modernisme and Noucentisme is this: One was an architecture meant for jewels — for extravagant villas, parks, and institutions commissioned by wealthy patrons such as Pau Gil and Eusebi Güell — and reliant on the Belle Époque equivalent of the starchitect. It was meant to be unusual and flashy. The other was an architecture meant for the regular texture of cities: elegant, understated constructions that relied on disciplined professionals and industrial production. Noucentista intellectuals criticized Modernisme as a fad, and their architects made public buildings such as schools and libraries.

It’s not inconceivable that, given enough time, an industrialized version of Art Nouveau would have arisen. Something analogous eventually happened with another ornamented style, Art Deco.15 But this raises the question of whether a hypothetical scaled-up Art Nouveau style, using standardized elements and well-defined principles, would have been recognizable as Art Nouveau. In any case, nowhere did Art Nouveau last long enough, or was applied at a large enough scale, for us to find out.

I have a half-baked theory that Art Nouveau was an instance of a broader phenomenon of excessive subcultures that tend to exhaust themselves in just a few years. Two examples from very different periods are the disco era of the 1970s and the phenomenon of incroyables and merveilleuses in the second half of the 1790s, toward the end of the French Revolution. In both cases, the subculture adopted an ethos of exaggeration, and the peak of the fashion lasted only four or five years.

Art Nouveau was a similarly short-lived, excessive fashion, except the part of it that consisted of architecture is still extant, since architecture usually tends to stick around. But there isn’t a lot of it, so its excesses are now charming oddities that attract tourists — which may be a better outcome than overwhelmingly decorated cities anyway.

Of course, the real reason we’re compelled to ask a question like “Why aren’t we living in an Art Nouveau world?” isn’t that we got a return to classicism instead. Proponents of the trad critique would love it if we still made classical (or, for that matter, Art Deco) buildings. The problem isn’t that Modernisme died; it’s that everything died except modernism (sans e).

What does the end of Art Nouveau teach us about this complicated problem?

First, it clarifies that classicism and Art Nouveau were very distinct, even opposed styles. It’s easy for amateurs of architecture history to conflate everything that came before modernism as “traditional.” But if you truly want some kind of return to historicism, it’s useful to know what you’re asking for. Wishing for an idiosyncratically decorated house by a starchitect is very different from encouraging regular real estate developers to build neighborhoods with a Mediterranean-inspired, humane scale. And if what you actually want is ornamentation, rather than classical columns or symmetry, it is possible in principle to explore this while rejecting traditionalism entirely.

The resurgence of classicism right after Art Nouveau also suggests a mechanism for the later dominance of modernism. I mentioned that classical architecture was a codified system, and that may be part of why it bounced back so fast. In the early 20th century, it was also the default style taught in schools, and it still carried the prestige of Greece and Rome. Classicism was an idea with strong staying power, and as a result it was easy for the patrons and institutions who commissioned buildings to retreat back to it.

Modern architecture developed a clear doctrine (form follows function; ornament is dishonest) and standardized components (like non-structural curtain walls and modular grids). It took advantage of industrial production and relaxed the bottleneck of bespoke handicraft, making modernist construction cheaper than that of Art Nouveau. But unlike the plain buildings of the past, which were cheap but signaled poverty, the new ones were prestigious, since they were what the innovative architects were working on. This combination made it a ruthlessly efficient meme, propagating as a new prestige idiom across universities but also trickling into ordinary construction projects. Under modernism, unlike Art Nouveau, you could build any house, apartment complex, store, or factory according to the new respectable paradigm without hiring an expensive architect. Thus, many traditional vernaculars were gradually pushed to the margins, giving way to a single global default.

I suspect the real reason modernism is so disliked is that it won too much. It is the totalization of this one style, more than its lack of decoration, that causes so much traditionalist angst. When the first modernist buildings appeared, as unusual jewels by innovative architects in ornamented cities, their minimalism was an interesting contrast. Now the reverse is true. So many cities, outside of their preserved historical cores, look the same. But the self-reinforcing cultural and economic system supporting modernism makes it hard to go back.

In Barcelona there is a curiosity that allows the visitor to experience the contrast just as the people of a century ago did. At the foot of the Montjuïc hill lies the Plaça d’Espanya, which was the site of the 1929 World’s Fair. Some of the area was built in the Noucentista style, some in eclectic monumentalism like the pompous Palau Nacional, now an art museum. But among the pavilions erected by participating countries was the German one, designed by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich. It was one of the first manifestations of what would be called the International Style, which would dominate mid-century modern architecture.

The German Pavilion is clean, geometric, and made of luxurious stones like marble and red onyx. There is something enjoyably calm about it after having visited the grandiose buildings of the Plaça d’Espanya and the overwhelming masterpieces of Gaudí and Domènech i Montaner. I completely understand why avant-garde architects of the time thought it represented the future. In fact, I might even venture to say that I like it more than Sant Pau and the Sagrada Família. I would sooner live in Mies van der Rohe’s house than the Casa Batlló.

The public of the World’s Fair didn’t really agree. Besides a few specialists praising it, the German Pavilion was mostly ignored amid the monumentalism of the Palau Nacional and the pleasant pastiche of the Poble Espanyol, where buildings typical of various regions of Spain had been built for show. The Pavilion was demolished the next year and mostly forgotten until it was recognized as a milestone in modern architecture and rebuilt in 1986. So we have to give the trad critics some credit: Modernism was less popular than ornate classicism even from its beginnings; the people of the 1920s were not particularly tired of ornamentation.

I further concede that entire cities built like this, except with more mundane materials, are not great. Planned modernist capitals like Brasília, or cities that were rebuilt in a modern style after being bombed — like many Japanese cities or Le Havre in France — are not usually considered dream destinations for their architectural beauty.16 Still, I grow annoyed at pronouncements that something like the German Pavilion is inherently ugly. It’s not! Many people quite like it, myself included, and many people at the time did too.

And around the world there are many other modern masterpieces — I’m quite fond of the brutalist Habitat 67, designed by Moshe Safdie in my own city of Montreal. Perhaps modernism, like Modernisme, was meant mostly for jewels, and it is an accident that it became so common for everything else.

Perhaps this conclusion makes sense because of another trait that modernism and Modernisme share, despite their totally opposite approaches to ornamentation. I’ve been treating the linguistic similarity as an annoying coincidence that I need to make sure won’t confuse readers, but it’s not really a coincidence. The two movements share, in addition to a desire for newness and a rejection of the historical catalogue, much of the same professional lineage.

As early as 1936, Nikolaus Pevsner in Pioneers of the Modern Movement traced a genealogical link between Art Nouveau and modernism. Not only were the main founders of modernism directly influenced by the ornamented style of the early 1900s, they practiced it themselves in some cases. Le Corbusier, known for Chandigarh in India and his plan to raze part of Paris and replace it with modernist skyscrapers, started out building chalets in a hyperlocal Art Nouveau variant called Style Sapin in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Switzerland.17 For a time, he also worked under Peter Behrens, who had been an influential Art Nouveau architect before pivoting to industrial design.

In Germany, the Bauhaus art school of Walter Gropius was formed by merging two existing schools, one of which had been founded by Henry van de Velde — one of the originators of Art Nouveau in Belgium. The Bauhaus inherited a lot of Art Nouveau’s principles, such as the rejection of academic historicism and the desire for well-designed everyday objects, while doing away with the organic ornament.18 It even began with a medieval and mystical stance: The cover to the 1919 manifesto by Gropius was a woodcut of a Gothic cathedral with glowing stars — not so different from the Sagrada Família!

Gropius also worked under Behrens a bit before 1910. And though Mies van der Rohe had a different background, he also overlapped with Gropius and Le Corbusier at the Behrens workshop.

We shouldn’t overstate the link between these traditions. Modern architecture had roots elsewhere too, and there is no reason to consider Art Nouveau’s evolution into ornamentless Bauhaus or International Style as inevitable. But I might have to qualify my earlier claim that we don’t know what a scaled-up, industrialized version of Art Nouveau would look like. In some sense, we know exactly what it looks like: it’s the world we have been inhabiting for the last hundred years. The original version of Art Nouveau was too bespoke, too excessive, too weird to last. Yet there was a way to both reject historicism and build at the scale of cities. The Bauhaus and Le Corbusier and Mies van der Rohe found it, and it worked so well it overtook classicism, Art Nouveau, Art Deco, and most local vernaculars after the Second World War.

Now we yearn for ornament again. The yearning is fine, and some companies promise to make it cheap with robotics and AI, so the wish may come true. Let’s just not fall into the trap of totalizing whatever ends up being the next architectural fashion, lest we get tired of it with no way out for decades.

This article originally appeared in Issue 16: Flourishing. Subscribe to the print magazine to get future issues delivered to your door.

1

Catalan Modernisme (adjective form: Modernista), which I’ll keep writing in italics, is distinct from what we usually call in English “modernism” or modern architecture. This distinction is important throughout the essay.

2

As of this year, you can now purchase a Lego set of the church for $800. Matching the ambition of the original, it is the largest Lego set in history at 12,060 pieces.

3

These national variations include Secession in Austria-Hungary; Modern Style in Britain; Jugendstil (“youth style”) in Germany, the Nordic countries, and Latvia; Liberty Style in Italy; Nieuwe Kunst (“new art”) in the Netherlands; and Tiffany Style in the United States.

4

The Barcelona Modernisme Route includes 120 buildings. The total number of Art Nouveau buildings is likely between several hundred and a few thousand, out of several tens of thousands of buildings in the city.

5

A fair amount of scholarly literature suggests that traditional architecture is more popular than modern architecture, though this is a difficult question to study and the answers vary quite a bit depending on context. Some of these surveys, such as a recent study by Mouratidis in Norway and Greece, are conducted by independent scholars, but others, like one by the National Civic Art Society, are commissioned by traditionalist advocacy organizations or political groups.

6

Samuel Hughes at Works in Progress has done interesting work exploring some of the explanations, such as the claim that ornament became too expensive in the industrial era.

7

Gran Enciclopèdia Catalana, s.v. “Hospital de Sant Pau“; Miquel Terreu, “Els plànols de la construcció de l’Hospital de la Santa Creu i Sant Pau,” De Santa Creu a Sant Pau, April 3, 2020.

8

The literature on the hedonic treadmill in architecture isn’t that clear. At least one study found an inverted-U relationship, where ratings of buildings improved and then declined as more time was spent in them (Cheuk Fan Ng, “Perception and Evaluation of Buildings: The Effects of Style and Frequency of Exposure,” Collabra: Psychology 6, no. 1 (2020): 44). But there isn’t a lot of evidence, and many factors come into play. Arthur Stamps (“Of Time and Preference: Temporal Stability of Environmental Preferences,” Perceptual and Motor Skills 85, no. 3 (1997): 883-96) found preferences stable over decades, while Jack Nasar (“Influence of Familiarity on Responses to Visual Qualities of Neighborhoods,” Perceptual and Motor Skills 51, no. 2 (1980): 635-42) found that familiarity lowered interest but raised pleasantness.

9

This reaction is mentioned on https://www.sseriga.edu/about/building, a page by the Stockholm School of Economics in Riga, which occupies one of the Eisenstein buildings.

10

See Jānis Krastiņš, “Riga: Walking in the Art Nouveau Metropolis,” Coup de Fouet, no. 4 (2004).

11

Peter Clericuzio, “Nancy as a Center of Art Nouveau Architecture, 1895-1914,” 2011.

12

Nou means both “nine” and “new” in Catalan.

13

Full quote: “Lo Arbitrari no és lo excéntrich, sinó, contràriament, lo con-céntrich, lo clàssich.” (“The Arbitrary is not the eccentric but, on the contrary, the concentric, the classical.”) D’Ors deliberately redefined arbitrariness as the willed imposition of human order, a core principle in his developing theory of Noucentisme. Eugeni d’Ors, “Glosari,” La Veu de Catalunya, August 29, 1906.

14

One exception to Art Nouveau’s irreplicability was the famous entrances to the Paris Metro by Hector Guimard, which featured the organic curves of the style but were mass-produced with cast iron.

15

Art Deco was an ornamented style, but its ornamentation was geometric enough to be replicable with industrial methods. Accordingly, it did scale considerably more into vernacular architecture, such as cinemas and apartment blocks. In contrast with Art Nouveau’s focus on nature, Art Deco was also a product of machine-age optimism. It embraced new materials like chromium plating and bakelite plastic. In fact, it wasn’t initially seen as a single style, but rather a collection of trends, some more decorative and luxurious, and others more industrial and streamlined. The contrast was already visible in the 1925 Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels Modernes, which retrospectively gave Art Deco its name in the 1960s. Some of these trends — stripped classicism, Streamline Moderne — also match Art Nouveau’s history of evolving toward classical or less ornamented variants.

16
