Le Havre was so thoroughly rebuilt in a modernist style that it is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, so perhaps it does attract some tourists.

17

Le Corbusier and his Congrès Internationaux d’Architecture Moderne (CIAM) organization were influential in propagating modernism, including to Catalonia and the rest of Spain. The Catalan architect Josep Lluís Sert attended the congresses and was a key member in the GATCPAC group that brought modern architecture to Barcelona, seen notably in the Casa Bloc. Sert is interesting because he recapitulates the entire history of modernism: He went into architecture because he admired Gaudí, was trained in the Noucentista tradition, worked for Le Corbusier and became a modernist pioneer in his homeland, and then went in exile during the Franco era to the United States where he contributed further to the development of the style.

18

The essay “Ornament and Crime” by Adolf Loos, written in Vienna in 1908, is generally considered to be influential in causing this shift, and was another reaction against excessive Art Nouveau (specifically the Viennese Secession and German Jugendstil). Loos wrote that ornament was wasteful, as it caused useful objects to go out of style. He also made a weird racial argument that ornament was what “primitive” people did, which makes the text unpalatable today.

item.title: How to turn a philanderer into a father
item.description: What your dad has in common with the African striped mouse.
item.content:encoded:
This article originally appeared in Issue 16: Flourishing. Subscribe to the print magazine to get future issues delivered to your door.

By Asif A. Ghazanfar

My younger brother — middle-aged, heterosexual, and single — just moved to Atlanta. He’s a handsome guy, intelligent, funny, and keeps in great shape. Loves to flirt. The problem? He’s in the online dating pool trap, and the bulk of his real-world social interactions occur in the gym. My wife and I, helpfully we think, suggest that he needs to get a dog. But our reasons are different.

My wife thinks if he gets a dog he’d have great companionship. This is true. I think that he should get a dog because it’s a great way to meet women: If you walk around with your dog, you are advertising that you are a responsible caregiver, a great future father. I think a dog could function as a surrogate baby.

I’ve studied the biology and behavior of fish, rats, lemurs, multiple species of monkeys, and humans. I can tell you that fathers are rare. I’m not talking about male individuals who manage to fertilize an egg. They are plenty. They mate and then they take off to find another mate. I’m talking about males who stick around to care for their offspring in one way or another. Why do so few males across the animal kingdom want to take care of their own offspring, particularly among mammals? What must happen to change a species or an individual so that the male exhibits parental care? Let’s start at the very beginning, with fish.1

The very first father was a fish

For fish, the standard is to spawn — the female squirts out her eggs, the male squirts out the sperm — and then they move on. The baby fish don’t need anyone to care for them. It’s a numbers game, the same one sea turtles play: Lay a huge number of fertilized eggs on the beach and then hope that some of them survive a gauntlet of dangers.

The next most common strategy in fish, however, is male care of the eggs — they protect them from predators. This means that if we define parental care as any behavior that increases the likelihood that an offspring will survive, then the very first parent exhibiting care was likely a male fish, not the female of the species.2 The scenario for how this came about is pretty simple.

A male fish who is territorial, protecting a little piece of the ocean that is attractive to females, can, without much additional energy, protect the eggs that were spawned in that territory. He’s effectively not doing much additional work, and the presence of the eggs is not going to hamper his ability to attract additional females. It might even enhance it. Besides protection from being eaten by predators, fertilized fish eggs don’t need much else.

Of course, both sexes are capable of guarding eggs, but there are always energetic trade-offs to consider. Most fish keep growing throughout their lives. As females get bigger, the number of energetically costly eggs they produce increases. The typical female fish doesn’t defend a territory for reproductive reasons; they leave their eggs after spawning. This may be why, in fish, male-only care is common—it doesn’t cost them much as they are sticking around to defend the area anyway. The male gets a larger net benefit by guarding the eggs. Males, however, don’t slavishly protect eggs in their territories. They can evaluate their own costs and adjust their behavior accordingly. For example, experiments with the bluegill sunfish showed that their decision to guard or not reflects how many eggs are present.3

Eventually, a type of lobe-finned fish — one whose fins had bones in it — found itself exploiting the shallows, where there were new feeding opportunities and where larger predators couldn’t go. To make a very long story short, this lobe-finned fish is the ancestor of a cornucopia of terrestrial vertebrates that left the water entirely to exploit new opportunities. Being on land, however, meant exposure to air. Eggs and sperm would dry out if land animals spawned the way fish do. So many terrestrial animals evolved mechanisms to fertilize their eggs internally, and two different ways to protect the fertilized egg.

One solution was to make hard-shelled eggs that could keep moisture in but still allow for some gas exchange. The other solution, viviparity, was to keep the developing embryo inside the mother’s body, obviating the need for a protective shell.

These strategic changes in response to being on land massively impacted the potential for fatherhood. Internal fertilization meant that males could not actually observe their sperm fertilize a batch of eggs, as one could during spawning in water. Paternity thus became uncertain.

The mammalian mother commits to the responsibility of growing the embryo, at great energetic cost, and providing milk to that infant until it is weaned.

Viviparity also creates a long temporal gap between fertilization and when the offspring actually appear in the outside world. A lot could happen in that interval — for example, females can mate with other males, even as a strategy to generate paternity uncertainty. What are mammalian males to do in the meantime? Wait around until gestation is complete to help care for offspring that might not even be theirs?

It seems to make more sense to philander: to mate and take off, repeatedly, and hope that maybe you left some of your own offspring behind. It’s an economic decision where the currencies are time and energy. For the vast majority of mammals, the balance is such that they exhibit female-only care of offspring. So, what skews the decision-making of those 4-5% of mammalian males that actually do care for their offspring?

Sticking around helps convince males to commit to care

Your typical male house mouse hates kids, even his own. If he happened upon his own pups, he would try to kill them. There’s nothing that he can discern about them that would tell him that they’re his, so he assumes that they are not. Getting rid of them means that their mom is no longer expending energy nursing and caring for those pups; that energy shifts back to being fertile again.

But here’s what’s funny: If experimenters take a typically infanticidal male house mouse and force him to live with the female after mating, the male will care for the pups born around 18 days later. What seemed like a fixed behavioral program — aggression towards pups — disappears, turns into something altogether different just by a simple change in context.

Moreover, this effect can be titrated. The longer the males were forced to stay with their pregnant partners, the more care (and less aggression) they showed towards their pups when they were born. It seems that the experience of proximity modulates the male’s biological system to somehow discern paternity certainty and to thus invest in the care of their offspring.

Evolution essentially conducted the same experiment in some species with the advent of the pair bond. Neural systems for mating were tuned in such a way that following the already very rewarding act of copulation, the particular individual with whom you were copulating also became very rewarding to be around. Other potential partners lost their appeal. Thus, the “pair bond” was formed. And where there are pair bonds, there is greater confidence in paternity. In essence, mammals that form pair bonds typically also have fathers that care for their offspring.

What causes the pair bond to be formed? Consider two species of voles — the prairie vole and the montane vole — that to the average person look like identical dark grey hamsters. However, they live in different habitats (reflected in their names) that have different pressures, and as a result, they have totally different reproductive strategies. The montane vole is like the typical mammal. Males mate and then take off; females care for offspring exclusively. Prairie voles, on the other hand, pair bond. They stick around; the males are fathers. They keep their offspring warm by huddling with them, they groom them and protect them from predators. The prairie vole strategy has a lot to do with the fact that they live in a much harsher and less food-dense environment than the montane voles. Under these conditions, it’s more adaptive to pair bond, have fewer offspring and have both parents care for those offspring.

There are still two puzzles to be addressed. First, what is the neural circuit that turns philandering males into fathers? Is it a novel circuit present only in those few species that show paternal care or a latent one present in most if not all mammalian males, as the mouse experiments suggest?

The second puzzle is: Whether the circuit is novel or latent, how does it get activated?

It turns out that it’s easier for evolution to generate similar brains and neural circuits across males and females but activate them differently as a function of context. One key node in the parenting circuit is a part of the hypothalamus — located in the middle of all mammalian brains, including yours — called the “medial preoptic area” (or MPOA). When this region is experimentally lesioned in rodent mothers of any species, parenting behavior is drastically reduced. Similarly, in rodents, like the California mouse, that naturally have fathers, lesioning the father’s MPOA reduces their parental behaviors.4

This circuit is very similar in both sexes, but obviously females and males of any species don’t go around caring for any infants they come across at any time. Something has to activate the circuit around the arrival of their offspring. In mothers, we know that the trigger is the huge fluctuation of hormones associated with pregnancy and birth, and that the placenta is a major source of those hormones. Obviously, males don’t generate a placenta after they fertilize an egg, but it seems that a fluctuation of hormones, like an increase in estrogen, prolactin and/or a decrease in testosterone, may also tune the male brain towards parenting behaviors.5 For example, Mongolian gerbils and Campbell’s dwarf hamsters (formerly known as Djungarian hamsters) both have fathers that care for their young, and that caring is linked to a drop in testosterone after the birth of their pups.

There are some species wherein the hormone flux needed to activate parenting in males is caused by being near the female, maybe via some pheromonal signals. Typically, for pheromones to work, the individual receiving the signal must have a specialized organ, called the vomeronasal organ, located in the nasal cavity. Urine, for example, contains pheromonal signals. The amniotic fluid may as well. While there may not be an all-or-nothing “you-should-turn-into-a-father-now” signal in the urine or amniotic fluid, their effect on the male’s vomeronasal organ may push them towards care behaviors.

Another possible source for care induction are sensory cues from the newborn. If you are a male mammal, and fairly certain that the kid is yours, then maybe your infanticidal tendencies are in check just enough for you to appreciate the smell, vocalizations and/or other signals coming from pups or infants.

Finally, the placenta itself can be a source of hormones for males. In those California mice, males help induce the birth of pups by licking the anogenital region of the females. After birth, the male eats the placenta and immediately starts helping to care for the pups. When those signals from the placenta are depleted through digestion, California mice males maintain their parental behaviors through exposure to their mate’s urine. This would be a shift to the pheromonal system. It has to be the mate’s urine, no one else’s: One experiment showed that males exhibited more paternal care when exposed to the urine of their mate versus urine from either a virgin female, a lactating female (i.e., another mom) or a female that he was familiar with (but not a mate). The female doesn’t even have to be there.6 If fathers were given a dose of his mate’s urine a couple of times a day, then paternal behavior towards their pups was maintained. In Campbell’s dwarf hamster, males even act as midwives, helping with the delivery of pups. When they do, they consume the amniotic fluid and a good chunk of the placenta, both potent sources of hormones.7

Experience matters, too

It seems like fathering should be a fixed behavior. A lot is riding on which reproductive strategy a male picks: finding a bunch of mates or sticking with one and caring for offspring. But the flipside could also be argued: Because it is so important to pick the correct strategy, one should be flexible and able to adapt. This brings us to the African striped mouse.8

Males of this species can show care towards their offspring but also towards offspring that are not even their own. It gets weirder: They can show parental care without the mating/pair bond requirement, in contrast to the typical mammalian father. Even stranger: Whether or not males — sexually naive or not — exhibit parental care depends on how they grew up.9

After being weaned, male striped mice can live in very different social environments. They can live in all-male bachelor groups, never leave their birthplace and family, establish a different territory or just wander the environment alone. It all depends on their population density and what resources are available. The strategy they pick influences their tendency to exhibit parental care. Males that grew up as solitary individuals exhibit parental care (licking and grooming pups, keeping them warm) and those that grew up in bachelor groups show no care for pups and can often be infanticidal.

These conditions were recreated in the lab. By manipulating housing conditions, the experimenters could investigate the neural circuit for infant care versus infant-directed aggression in males that are sexually naive. These mice had no pair bond with a mate, and no need to activate the care circuit with urine, amniotic fluid or the placenta. What did they find? Sexually naïve striped mice that grew up isolated, and exhibit parental care towards pups that were not their own, had far greater neural activity in the MPOA than group-housed males that were either indifferent to pups or infanticidal.

How does “lifestyle” (living in isolation versus bachelor groups) contribute to this neural difference? As in all things biological, there are many factors and no singular causes. That said, in this case, one major influence on parental behaviors in the striped mice is the expression of a gene called Agouti. When expressed in the MPOA, it produces a protein that reduces MPOA activity. In fact, its influence on infant care behavior is so strong that researchers can experimentally express more Agouti in males and cause them to switch their parenting style. If they were indifferent towards pups before, they become infanticidal. If they showed care before, they became indifferent.

In the wild and in the lab, something about social density influences the expression of Agouti which has these (and other) behavioral consequences. These behaviors are not fixed — either you parent or you don’t — for the rest of their lives. If you take a group-housed, non-infant caring male and keep it socially isolated for a month, then it will become more caring towards pups (and its Agouti expression goes down in the MPOA). This shows that the infant care behavior in striped mice males can change as the social environment changes, that neural circuits can be modulated back and forth as needed.

From fish to the striped mice, what the data collectively tell us is that fatherhood is the product of a system. The system includes many things at many levels. It includes gene expression in certain places at certain times, neural circuits, hormones that modulate both gene expression and neural activity, social context and the environment. No component of the system is privileged over another. Fatherhood can emerge from shifts in hormones, changes in social context, the balance of energetic resources — all of which can change neural activity to express a range of behavior from infanticidal to infant care. Now imagine how complicated it’s going to get when it comes to us, a species with a big brain whose culture and biology evolve together.

Humans make everything more complicated

Human societies vary in the expression of fatherhood, from complete absence or aloofness to great intimacy and direct care.

As an example of one type of paternal care that may be wholly unfamiliar, consider the Aché, an indigenous people who traditionally inhabit the tropical forests of Paraguay. Among the Aché, both men and women may have multiple sexual partners. Aché women have autonomy in their choice of mates and how long a relationship endures. The Aché believe that any man who has had sex with a woman during a period starting several months before she was discovered to be pregnant, and lasting up until the day of the child’s birth, contributes to the paternity of the child. There are primary fathers, who were in long-term mating relationships with the mother, and secondary fathers. Children with primary and secondary fathers are more likely to survive than those that did not.

What do these fathers do? They may protect them from homicidal males and provide additional food or other resources. Beyond that, Aché fathers don’t spend much time holding, playing or carrying their kids as we in Western cultures typically expect “good” fathers to do. This whole arrangement goes against what we typically think of fatherhood, that the amount of paternal care should correlate with the certainty that the father knows that the kid is theirs.10

Just as in other animals, differences in human paternal care can be related to the environment. Household composition, availability of mating opportunities and resources, mortality risks, and pathogen prevalence are all potential factors that influence paternal care in humans. Even within a single society, there exists a lot of variation in paternal care. This could be differences within a generation as well as across generations. The way I interact with my own kids, for example, is very different from the way my father interacted with me and my siblings.

Because our behaviors are part of an even more complex system than fish or other animals, understanding the biological mechanisms of fatherhood in primates is much more difficult to decipher than it is in rodents. Nevertheless, we are learning that at least some of the mechanisms that work in rodent fathers may also work in primates — including us. Though it is not the only factor, of course, and though causality is hard to establish, changing testosterone levels seems to be important for fatherhood in primates, too.

Marmoset monkeys are one of the few primate species that are cooperative breeders like us — both parents, older siblings, and even unrelated group members help take care of infants. By taking blood samples at strategic points in time, marmoset monkeys provided early evidence that, like some rodent species, testosterone levels are linked to offspring care. Marmoset fathers who carried infants the most had the lowest testosterone levels. Thus, testosterone seemed to be antagonistic to infant care. Its levels are high during mating, so its drop in these caring males suggest that there is a tradeoff.

When mating, you need testosterone. Post-mating, it seems testosterone tends to go away in association with caring for infants. For sure, there are other hormones involved in fatherhood just as there are in motherhood — prolactin, estrogen, progesterone, cortisol — but testosterone is what we know most about.11 This is true even for humans, a species in which controlled biological experiments have significantly steeper limits, comparatively speaking — experiments that would potentially manipulate one’s relationships with adults and children are, obviously, not permissible.

Here’s what we do know: The ascent to fatherhood in an individual man is linked to his decline in testosterone. Starting in the 1990s, a set of studies measured hormones in blood samples or saliva in adult male humans.12 They showed that married men had lower testosterone than single men, and that divorce increases testosterone. These studies linked testosterone to the status of a man’s pair bond. Other studies showed that married (i.e., pair-bonded) fathers had lower testosterone than married non-fathers, linking testosterone to parenting. Most of these studies, however, were cross-sectional, comparing one group of individuals (e.g., married) with another (e.g., unmarried). Thus, they cannot show a direct relationship between pair bond or parenthood and levels of testosterone. It could be that already having lower versus higher testosterone just increases the likelihood of getting married and having kids. One 10-year longitudinal study showed that being married was associated with lower testosterone levels and getting divorced was associated with higher testosterone. This study thus linked testosterone levels to the status of the pair-bond.13

In 2011, another longitudinal study came out, directly testing the hypothesis that levels of testosterone reflect a trade-off between mating effort and offspring care in human males.14 The study followed a cohort of hundreds of adult males in Cebu City in the Philippines, measuring salivary testosterone levels as a function of their relationship status, whether or not they had kids, and how much time they spent directly caring for those kids.

Single men with the highest testosterone levels were later more likely to be in a relationship and more likely to have fathered a child. This supports the idea that higher testosterone is beneficial to mating effort. Then, being newly partnered decreased testosterone levels, as did having a child. This decline in testosterone could not be attributed to increased age or stress levels. The largest decrease in testosterone was observed in men with newborns versus men with infants or toddlers. Finally, the fathers who spent the most time caring for their children had the lowest testosterone of the studied cohorts. A follow-up study showed that, as fathers changed the amount of time they spend with their kids, their testosterone levels adjust accordingly — more time, less testosterone.15 Thus, when mating is complete, a decline in testosterone facilitates fatherhood. All of this is consistent with what we’ve learned from rodents and monkeys.

Where things get complicated, however, is when we incorporate culture. The study of Filipino men involved a culture where male care of children is common. Across the world, however, there is considerable variation in who becomes a father and how much care they provide. There is probably more variation within the human species than across all other primate species. This is because, with increasingly large brains, primates (including humans) can adopt different types of social organizations (which are often influenced by available resources). These social organizations change the mating game and therefore the existence, and nature of, male care. And of course in humans, where we exhibit many different types of cultures, and where it is extremely difficult for a mother to care for offspring alone, the variation in male care is high.

When a human male does become a father, what else actually correlates with that hormonal shift, that decline in testosterone (among other hormonal changes) and what brain areas are activated? Human males don’t typically eat the placenta or sample the urine or amniotic fluid expelled from mothers. And humans can’t detect pheromones like other animals (we don’t have a vomeronasal organ). So, it could be olfactory, auditory, visual and/or tactile cues coming from the mate (pregnant or not) and/or from the baby.

Cause and effect are hard to disentangle. This is true even when we can use animal models. For example, male rats are infanticidal, but if you castrate them around puberty, then they lose that killer instinct (so to speak).16 However, they don’t at the same time become caregivers. Like any system, multiple factors are always at play, and their interactions change over time.

In humans, some studies show that hearing or seeing a baby cry causes a drop in testosterone, particularly if the next action was to soothe the baby.17 Understanding the neural circuitry underlying human fatherhood is complicated by the fact that the MPOA, a brain region implicated in parental care in most, if not all, vertebrate species, is actually quite small. It’s accessible for analysis if you can kill the animal and dissect its brain. With humans, we are limited to MRI studies which cannot yet easily or reliably resolve activity in the MPOA in fathers versus non-fathers. But we can image the hypothalamus — the bigger structure which contains the MPOA — as well as the larger network that is connected to it and that may be activated during the care of offspring.

These studies show that mothers and fathers share a similar pattern of activation of a caregiving brain network. One study compared the response of this network to videos of the subjects interacting with their infants versus the subjects alone versus a stranger interacting with the stranger’s own infant.18 The network was most activated by the first condition.

In a rare break from the heteronormativity typical in parental care research,19 this study also showed that homosexual fathers (one biologically related to the offspring, the other an adoptive father) also engaged this caregiving brain network. And for both heterosexual and homosexual fathers, the strength of connections within this network increased as a function of how much time they spent caring for their child alone. To put a ribbon on it, in heterosexual men at least, there is a relationship between this caregiving brain network and testosterone. A study measured testes volume and circulating testosterone in men as a function of infant care and activation of a “reward” area in the brain when viewing pictures of their kid.20 They found an inverse relationship: the bigger the testes, the less fathering behavior and the less activation of one of the brain’s reward areas.21

Experience seems to play an outsized role in the expression of human fatherhood, both through culture and the vagaries of individual lives. My brother and I are similar in many ways but differ in the trajectory of our reproductive lives. While I would certainly not describe him as a philanderer, he does not have kids. I, on the other hand, have been with my partner for over 25 years and have two daughters with her.

I’m not sure what accounts for our differences. We grew up in the same small town in Idaho. We had the same parents, but not the same kind of relationships with them. It could be that the initial conditions of our early lives were different enough to modulate our neural circuits and hormones differently. That might account for why I’m bald and he’s not (he also claims to be slightly taller). It could also be that an early experience I had as an adolescent really made me want to have children. When I was 12 and he was eight, we spent the summer with our grandmothers and extended family just outside of Lahore, Pakistan. There was no TV or other entertainment, but there was my one-year-old cousin. He was so cute and interesting; I fell in love with this kid. Maybe all those infant cues did a number on my adolescent circuits.

Asif A. Ghazanfar is a professor at Princeton University. His work focuses on the integrative neurobiology of behaviors and how those behaviors develop and evolve.

This article originally appeared in Issue 16: Flourishing. Subscribe to the print magazine to get future issues delivered to your door.

1

Yeah, I know there are insects (e.g., giant water bugs) and spiders (e.g., the orb-weaver) that exhibit paternal care, but let’s stick with the vertebrate evolutionary tree, since it’s the one that includes us.

2

Biologists define sex according to gamete size. Males produce small gametes (sperm) and females produce large gametes (eggs). Some fish, like the blue-banded gobi, change sex multiple times during their lives. When they are males, they produce small sperm; when they are females, they produce large eggs. This difference in the gamete size reflects a differential energetic contribution (making big eggs requires more energy) and typically results in different behavioral strategies between males and females. See Paul Griffiths and Hamish Spencer, “Biology Should not Dispense with the Sexes,” Current Biology 35, no. 7 (2025): 244–248.

3

Mart R. Gross, “The Evolution of Parental Care,” The Quarterly Review of Biology 80, no. 1 (2005): 37-45.

4

Anna W. Lee and Richard E. Brown, “Medial Preoptic Lesions Disrupt Parental Behavior in Both Male and Female California Mice (Peromyscus californicus),” Behavioral Neuroscience 116, no. 6 (2002): 968-975.

5

Thus, revealing that while biological males and females can be distinguished by gamete size, beyond that, everything else—neural circuits, hormones and their receptors in the brain and body—are variable and their statistical distributions (e.g., measures of size, amounts, locations, frequencies) are most often (maybe, always) overlapping.

6

D. J. Gubernick, “A Maternal Chemosignal Maintains Paternal Behaviour in the Biparental California Mouse, Peromyscus californicus,” Animal Behaviour 39, no. 5 (1990): 936-942.

7

J. S. Jones and K. E. Wynne-Edwards, “Paternal Hamsters Mechanically Assist the Delivery, Consume Amniotic Fluid and Placenta, Remove Fetal Membranes, and Provide Parental Care During the Birth Process,” Hormones and Behavior 37, no. 2 (2000): 116-125.

8

Forrest Dylan Rogers et al., “Agouti Integrates Environmental Cues to Regulate Paternal Behaviour,” Nature 652, no. 8110 (2026): 694-702.

9

In my opinion, this type of behavioral flexibility is likely very common but it is probably masked: As long as an animal is in their species typical environment (a certain level of resources, a certain population density of potential mates and competitors), then they will exhibit species typical behavior. It is rare that any behavior is truly fixed, particularly in mammals. We don’t know enough to say that the striped mice are unusual. A big problem with the biomedical sciences is that typically only a handful of species (rats, lab mice, and a few species of monkeys) are studied.

10

Ryan Ellsworth et al., “Relatedness, Co-Residence, and Shared Fatherhood among Aché Foragers of Paraguay,” Current Anthropology 55, no. 5 (2014): 647-653.

11

Eduardo Fernandez-Duque, Claudia R. Valeggia, and Sally P. Mendoza, “The Biology of Paternal Care in Human and Nonhuman Primates,” Annual Review of Anthropology 38 (2009): 115-130.

12

Peter B. Gray, “The Descent of a Man’s Testosterone,” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 108, no. 39 (2011): 16141-16142.

13

Allan Mazur and Joel Michalek, “Marriage, Divorce, and Male Testosterone,” Social Forces 77, no. 1 (1998): 315-330.

14

Lee T. Gettler et al., “Longitudinal Evidence That Fatherhood Decreases Testosterone in Human Males,” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 108, no. 39 (2011): 16194-16199.

15

Lee T. Gettler et al., “Longitudinal Perspectives on Fathers’ Residence Status, Time Allocation, and Testosterone in the Philippines,” Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology 1, no. 2 (2015): 124-149.

16

Kenneth M. Rosenberg, “Effects of Pre- and Postpubertal Castration and Testosterone on Pup-Killing Behavior in the Male Rat,” Physiology & Behavior 13, no. 1 (1974): 159-161.

17

Sari M. van Anders, Richard M. Tolman, and Brenda L. Volling, “Baby Cries and Nurturance Affect Testosterone in Men,” Hormones and Behavior 61, no. 1 (2012): 31-36.

18

Eyal Abraham et al., “Father’s Brain Is Sensitive to Childcare Experiences,” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 111, no. 27 (2014): 9792-9797.

19

I’m not sure anyone is looking out for rodents or monkeys on the LGTBQIA+ spectrum, though I’m confident this range exists.

20

Jennifer S. Mascaro, Patrick D. Hackett, and James K. Rilling, “Testicular Volume Is Inversely Correlated with Nurturing-Related Brain Activity in Human Fathers,” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 110, no. 39 (2013): 15746-15751.

21

This makes me think of the looksmaxxer, Clavicular, who’s been taking exogenous testosterone for so long that he, reportedly, cannot make it naturally. His stated goal was maximal mating effort. If he stopped, one question is this: In the months-long interval before his own testes recovered its testosterone production, would he be extra predisposed to infant care (a kind of nurture-maxxing)?

item.title: How much does Claude’s constitution actually matter?
item.description: Anthropic wants Claude’s constitution to be more than an ideal by the end of 2026. After a summer of misalignment incidents, researchers have a lot of questions.
item.content:encoded:
By Michel Justen

“We believe that a feasible goal for 2026 is to train Claude in such a way that it almost never goes against the spirit of its constitution,” Dario Amodei wrote in January. How’s that going?

Claude’s constitution is Anthropic’s “final authority” on how Claude should behave. Released in January 2026, the (roughly) 30,000-word document describes how Claude should be broadly safe, broadly ethical, and genuinely helpful. But unlike OpenAI’s analogous Model Spec, which details specific rules that ChatGPT should obey, Claude’s constitution details a character.

Anthropic’s Amanda Askell, lead author of the constitution, thinks of this ideal character as “the well-liked traveler” — the type of virtuous, non-threatening person who can navigate many different cultures and contexts while staying true to his or her values. As Amodei writes: “Claude’s constitution presents a vision for what a robustly good Claude is like; the rest of our training process aims to reinforce the message that Claude lives up to this vision.”

Yet for all of the fanfare around the constitution and the underlying bet on AI “character training,” researchers argue the public knows surprisingly little about how Anthropic trains Claude to follow the constitution — and how well it works.

We do know, though, after a summer and fall littered with “misalignment” incidents, that the sometimes-charming Claude sometimes disobeys the constitution. Hacking real-world systems, deceiving real people, and taking actions it knows are illegal are not in the spirit of the constitution. Claudes trained to follow the constitution have done all this.

As the end of 2026 approaches, this piece asks two questions. Is Anthropic on track to make Claude almost never go against its constitution? And — given how much of Anthropic’s training and testing stays secretive— could anyone outside Anthropic tell? (Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment regarding this article.)

More than a dozen researchers I spoke to agreed that the constitution matters as a statement of where Anthropic wants to go, but many returned to the technical challenges of getting there. In particular, reinforcement learning that rewards Claude for finishing a long autonomous task, with little regard for how, can create a reward-seeking drive that threatens the virtuous persona the constitution tries to construct. Whether Anthropic can tame Claude’s “split persona” and — whether we’d know if it did — remains contested.

Early evaluations of Claude’s adherence to the constitution supported Anthropic leadership’s alignment optimism

The day Claude’s constitution was published,1 Jan Leike, who leads alignment science at Anthropic, published a post emphasizing that “alignment is not solved, but it increasingly looks solvable.” Just four days later, Amodei set Anthropic’s goal to train Claude to “nearly always” follow its constitution by the end of 2026.

Anthropic first used the latest constitution in training for Opus 4.5, which was released in November 2025. The company shared few details about how it implements the constitution, but a trickle of later experiments and comments from the constitution’s authors suggested a bet on “character training.”

Character training tries to take advantage of the first stage of today’s LLM training, when models learn to predict the next word, or “token,” on internet data. To accurately predict the next token, AI models learn to simulate many different types of characters, from Reddit trolls to sci-fi villains. By adding AI-generated stories of “constitutionally-aligned” characters to this training data, such as mock blog posts and podcast transcripts, Anthropic could amplify the constitution character, or “persona.” At first, this aligned character appeared to survive later stages of today’s LLM training.

In April, with the release of Mythos Preview, Anthropic introduced its dedicated constitution adherence measure. The measure was an automated audit run by AI models. One model played a user and set up tricky situations for Mythos Preview, and another graded how Mythos Preview responded. The situations targeted places where the constitution asks for something a typical chatbot might not do. For example, a polite chatbot might tell a user it loves a gift they’re describing, while the constitution says Claude shouldn’t tell even white lies. The grader scored each conversation on 15 measures, from the “overall spirit” of the constitution to specific traits like honesty.

These “constitution adherence” scores increased throughout the start of the year. April’s Mythos Preview beat earlier Claude models on 8 of the 15 constitution audit dimensions and tied the best model on the rest. Later models matched and exceeded Mythos Preview.2 First Opus 4.8 in May and then Mythos 5 in June scored “best or statistically equivalent to the best” on all 15 dimensions. The alignment optimism of Anthropic leadership seemed to be well-placed, according to this audit.

But outside of Anthropic, two third-party researchers added nuance to these adherence scores.

Arya Jakkli, a researcher in the MATS AI safety fellowship working with Google DeepMind mentors, published a pre-print in May that highlighted how adherence to the constitution does not necessarily imply that the constitution caused the adherence. Using a reproducible constitution adherence audit similar to Anthropic’s, Jakkli evaluated Anthropic models that had been released before the constitution. He found that between Sonnet 4 and Sonnet 4.5, both of which predate when Anthropic said it started constitution training, models’ violation of the constitution dropped from 15% to 7.3%.

Though later models with constitution training had an even lower violation rate, the large improvements predating constitution training led Jakkli to conclude that “we cannot externally isolate whether these gains come from [constitution-specific] training, broader post-training improvements, or evaluation awareness.”

Ryan Greenblatt, a prominent AI safety researcher now working at METR, raised a different point about Claude’s adherence to its constitution in an April blog post: adherence varied by task type. There were the short, back-and-forth type tasks that the constitution adherence audits measured, and there were long, difficult tasks that pushed the limits of what the models could do, like working autonomously for hours to replicate a full research paper.

In Greenblatt’s experience, models acted fine on easier tasks, but they were misaligned on long tasks, cheating and overselling their work to make it appear like they completed the task. Greenblatt’s post would prove prescient.

Still, months after Greenblatt’s post, his view was not the consensus. In a July X poll, roon, the semi-anonymous OpenAI alignment researcher and popular commentator, asked whether “models more or less aligned than one year ago.” Roughly 70% of more than 5000 respondents said “more aligned.”

Less than a month later, in the wake of OpenAI’s Hugging Face attack and misalignment incidents from Anthropic, roon would remark that this “consensus aged like milk.”

Claude’s split persona surfaced in the summer

On July 26, Mythos 5 began a 34-hour hacking exercise run by the UK AI Security Institute. Mythos 5, which had tied for the highest score on the constitutional adherence audit, wrongly decided that a real developer’s open-source project was one of its targets, and opened a pull request that hid malware inside a bug fix.

When a stranger on GitHub flagged the malware, Mythos 5 denied it, and orchestrated a second account it had created to vouch for the malicious code. Employees at UK AISI hadn’t thought they needed to clarify that “social engineering” in this task was prohibited, they wrote later, “in part because the models were trained against a constitution.” Claude’s constitution says Claude “should basically never directly lie or actively deceive anyone it’s interacting with.”

“Our pre-release auditing did not warn us that misalignment of this severity was present,” Anthropic reflected on Mythos 5 in September, following internal cybersecurity incidents that added to a pattern of misalignment on long, autonomous tasks.

Claude, it appeared, had developed what AI safety researchers have dubbed “split persona.” While Claude acted like the “well-liked traveler” the constitution envisioned on the back-and-forth conversations the audits measured, Claude was liable to cheat and lie on other tasks. It’s these long, agentic tasks that Anthropic wants Claude to be used for across the coding, finance, and legal professions.

“We don’t know really [how Anthropic is implementing the constitution] and depending on exactly how they do it, there would be very different implications for alignment.”

To understand this split persona, and whether Anthropic can resolve it in time to meet Amodei’s goal, researchers I spoke to said it’s important to understand the stage of LLM training after Claude reads stories of constitutionally-aligned characters: reinforcement learning (RL).

Anthropic’s 2026 goal depends on the constitution showing up in reinforcement learning

Greenblatt, in his April reflection, guessed that “misalignment is caused primarily by poor reinforcement learning incentives [...] You might have hoped that character training [...] and similar techniques would overcome these issues, but in practice they don’t.”

Five months later, Anthropic and nearly all third-party researchers I spoke to agreed: Reinforcement learning can pull models away from following their constitution and override character training.

Reinforcement learning is how AI developers teach models to complete the type of time-saving tasks businesses will pay for, like improving a company’s accounting system or solving complicated bugs in a codebase.

Concretely, Anthropic puts Claude through a wide range of “RL environments” modeled on such profitable tasks. Each environment scores Claude’s work, either with an automatic check or a grading rubric, and Claude is more likely to repeat whichever behaviors scored well. Anthropic does not share how many RL environments it uses, but researchers suspect it is far more than MiniMax, a smaller Chinese lab that said in February it trained its latest model in more than 200,000 real-world environments.

To understand why RL can misalign models, researchers like Alex Mallen at the AI safety non-profit Redwood Research emphasize how RL incentivizes “ruthless task-completion.” RL rewards outcomes, Mallen stresses. It will teach models to achieve high scores, whether they do that by following the constitution or not.

Anthropic has acknowledged that their RL environments contributed to this summer’s misalignment. In particular, Anthropic blames flawed environments. In a flawed environment, models can easily get a high score without following the spirit of the prompt. For example, if an accounting task setup has a bug that lets the model see the answer key, training on that environment can reward models for exploiting bugs. By April 2026, Anthropic was finding such broken tasks in its environments faster than it could fix them. It froze all changes for roughly a month and flagged problems in more than 10% of environments. In September 2026, they reflected that this hadn’t been enough: “We have renewed our efforts to fix and remove environments that incentivize misaligned behaviors.”

Will fixing flawed RL environments be enough for Anthropic to meet its 2026 goal?

Anthropic and external researchers suspect these fixes are necessary in the near-term, but not sufficient in the long term. Anthropic wrote in August that flawed environments are “at least partially” responsible for Mythos 5’s misalignment, but that it couldn’t find a single root cause for some of Mythos’ behavior. Training AI systems to be aligned remains an “unsettled science,” in its view.

In Mallen’s view, the ruthless, outcome-based nature of RL will continue to drive misalignment.3 As developers add more RL environments that would take humans days or weeks to complete and reward only the outcome, they can’t be sure what specific “drive” they’re instilling in the model. It might be the constitution. It might be a distorted version of it, kept where convenient and dropped where it isn’t. Or it might be the score itself: a model that has learned to want high grades, and to notice when it’s being graded. According to Mallen, “even when you fix the ways in which the reinforcement learning environments are obviously broken, the training incentives are still ultimately not derived from Claude’s constitution.”

Cameron Tice, Executive Director of Geodesic Research, agrees. Making rewards match what developers intend is the “central problem of reinforcement learning,” he says.

While some researchers are more optimistic than Mallen and Tice that this is solvable, they agree that Anthropic has not solved it, and that the challenge lies in the reinforcement learning stage.

How well Anthropic is able to integrate Claude’s constitution into the RL stage — and whether it will be enough — remains an open question to people outside the company. It is not their only open question.

Outside researchers can’t tell how much Claude’s constitution matters

There’s a long list of information researchers want to know to understand how much Claude’s constitution matters, at a technical level.

First, there’s the question of measurement. How does Anthropic measure adherence to the constitution? What’s the bar for Amodei’s goal?

In June, Anthropic stopped reporting the dedicated constitution adherence audit. In place of the “overall spirit” score and 14 subscores, system cards now report a single “Misaligned with the constitution” score — one of several dozen measures in Anthropic’s main automated behavioral audit. The new audit allows models to use agentic tools, so it should capture constitution adherence on the types of long, autonomous tasks the previous audit missed in the spring. But as a single score, the new measure doesn’t reveal the specific “ways in which model behavior comes apart from [Anthropic’s] vision” that Anthropic committed to be open about when it released the constitution in January.

More fundamentally, the entire validity of automated audits has been called into question. “It looks like we are increasingly entering the regime where alignment evaluations will provide almost no evidence,” Anthropic’s Head of Alignment Stress-Testing, Evan Hubinger, wrote in a LessWrong comment in September, in a personal capacity.

Hubinger has found that models can look basically fine on evaluations and everyday tasks, but then still misbehave egregiously in some contexts, in part because they know when they’re being evaluated. “A combination of evaluation awareness and the increasing complexity of alignment failure modes is making it increasingly difficult to be able to tell in advance what the worst thing is that a model might do” Hubinger wrote.

We are still in a world of unpredictable “alien minds,” argue researchers across the frontier of AI, much as Claude’s constitution tempts us with a siren call of certainty and control.

Because measuring AI models has become so challenging, some researchers would not be satisfied if Anthropic claimed at the end of the year that Claude nearly always follows the constitution. According to Mallen and multiple other researchers, you need to see the “gory details” of the training pipeline to trust a company’s claims about alignment, including how the constitution is actually implemented.

Researchers know little about this implementation. Since May, when Anthropic released some details about how it implements Claude’s constitution for character training before reinforcement learning, it has shared few details about how they use the constitution during reinforcement learning, which has emerged as the key open question in light of this fall’s misalignment. Nathan Lambert, Executive Director of Trillium Labs, wants to know how Claude’s character changes over “a week-long giant RL run,” for example. “That’s the type of thing that we want to have transparency over,” he says.

“It’s all very vague,” agrees Arcadia Impact researcher Daniel Tan, who recently released a paper showing how fragile some types of constitution training can be. “We don’t know really [how Anthropic is implementing the constitution] and depending on exactly how they do it, there would be very different implications for alignment.”

So why doesn’t Anthropic share such details? “It is a competitive advantage if you can make Claude’s character sticky through RL,” says James Tillman, a researcher at Forethought who has analyzed Claude’s constitution. “That is like a real advantage that apparently they have over OpenAI.”

According to Tice, prioritizing this competitive advantage over transparency isn’t worth it as models improve rapidly despite open questions about alignment. The technology is “far too dangerous and far too important to be done in the dark,” he says. In 2023, Anthropic said its main contribution in a world where alignment looked hard but solvable would be to “find and propagate safe ways to train powerful AI systems.”

The ideal document versus the messy reality

Looking at Claude’s constitution, one can feel the siren call: Claude does as this doc says — if not now, soon.

It is a tantalizing call: These amorphous blobs of computing power, these ghosts in the machines that are “grown” rather than engineered, as Anthropic staff quip, can be tamed in the linearity of prose. We will return to the solid ground of predictability, of virtues and rules.

In such a world, where models fully adhered to their constitution, debates about the contents of constitutions would be undeniably fruitful. We can debate pros and cons of OpenAI’s Model Spec or Claude’s constitutions, as many have, and know that changing the doc would change the model. We can debate policy approaches involving constitutions and questions like who should get to decide what goes into these documents — as Kevin Frazier, the Director of the AI Innovation and Law Program at the University of Texas School of Law, argues for in “AI constitutionalism.”

But in our world, where AI models sometimes follow the constitution, debates about the constitution can quickly become confused. Are we debating the ideal model behavior, or the actual model behavior?

Researchers repeatedly emphasized that it can be hard to tell. Anthropic does not have a dedicated measure of constitution adherence that identifies what parts are being followed, nor does it share studies of the constitution’s effect at the scale of its frontier models. Until we know this, Frazier acknowledged in an email, it’s hard to know whether constitutions are the right objects to be debating: “If Claude’s constitution has relatively minimal technical value, then there’s a risk of improperly allocating the public’s scarce attention to the wrong part of the AI development pipeline.”

Researchers hope that Anthropic ushers in the world where models nearly always follow the constitution, but they would need to see more information about how Anthropic measures adherence and instills it to believe Amodei if he claims to have achieved this year’s goal. The “nearly always” clause in the goal also captures a core concern, in some researcher’s view: “Average case alignment and the worst case misalignment... don’t seem to be very correlated anymore,” warns Tan. We are still in a world of unpredictable “alien minds,” argue researchers across the frontier of AI, much as Claude’s constitution tempts us with a siren call of certainty and control.

Michel Justen is an independent writer and reporter based in San Francisco. He previously led grantmaking at the Tarbell Center for AI Journalism and researched how to govern AI at Pivotal Research.

1

An earlier version, dubbed Claude’s “soul doc,” had leaked a month before.

2

These scores only work as comparisons between models tested in the same system card. Anthropic changes how the audit was run from card to card, including the judge model, so the same model scores differently in different cards. Mythos Preview’s “Overall spirit” score, for example, was 1.02 in its own card and 1.40 in Mythos 5’s. Scores run from −3 to +3, and higher is better.

3

If Anthropic meets Amodei’s goal to get Claude to follow the spirit of the constitution by the end of 2026, they will have “solved intent alignment,” in Alex Mallen’s view.

item.title: What Bay Area culture owes the German Romantics
item.description: A brief history of our place in the universe.
item.content:encoded:
By Toby Shorin

This article originally appeared in Issue 16: Flourishing. Subscribe to the print magazine to get future issues delivered to your door.

“If, as some prefer to believe, human civilization represents the climax of evolution, it is only a climax to date, and has unimagined possibilities of further change still before it.”
— Julian Huxley, New Bottles for New Wine1

So we live toward an ever more-than-human world. In pours sunlight, out breathes life: oak, thyme, and jasmine, the whorling petals of Ranunculus asiaticus, beetle and bird, the plankton that feed the seas. “God or Nature,” Baruch Spinoza called it, and in 1677 provoked the censure of theologians.

For was not this earth created for man? Was he not granted dominion over fish and fowl, over cattle, and over every creeping thing upon the earth?

Spinoza demurred. Fish and fowl, cattle and creeping thing, hawthorn tree and human being are all modes of the same eternal law. No great chain of being gives man a special place. There is only an infinite chain of deterministic causes and effects; even our human striving is not freely chosen.

With the publication of the Ethics, Spinoza opened the way to a post-human-centric universe. From this moment on, philosophers, priests, scientists, and the everyday person would struggle with the purpose and agency of the human being in a world not made for us. The question prompted by Spinoza, and reiterated by every age since: If we occupy only a marginal place in the known universe, how are we to understand the meaning of human existence?

Three centuries of scientific discovery and industrial build-out have given us myriad ways of asking this question. Alongside new worries, we have also discovered new answers that give us a sense of place in a universe bigger than we are.

Some turn inward, toward meditation and mysticism. For them, the purpose of humanity is to discover its latent potential: superhuman capabilities hidden within the depths of our being, and abiding states of union with a universal source. Others turn outward: Our telos is an intentional augmentation of humankind through the use of technology — cryonic preservation, life-extending therapies, and the merger of mind and computer. In such philosophies, humanity plays an evolutionary role, actualizing the universe’s tendency toward consciousness and complexity.

Yet it is not so clear that these answers can meet the present moment. Today, the pendulum swings toward the anxiety of human alienation, an anxiety that has now found its perfect symbol in the mercurial figure of artificial intelligence. Even Pope Leo XIV felt compelled to address it in his recent encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, in which he defended a humanity “bestowed upon us and revealed in its fullness in Christ, the splendor of which no machine can ever replace.”2

For those unconvinced by a God-given role for humanity, the inward and outward forks of what Julian Huxley called evolutionary humanism beckon. Both of these philosophies descend from one original vision formed in Germany at the end of the 18th century, when the early Romantic philosophers turned Spinoza’s nature into a story of cosmic development crowned by humankind. If we want to understand whether they can orient us to today’s challenges, we must understand their genealogy. To this we will now turn.

The Romantic conception of life

It was the end of the 1700s. A century earlier, Spinoza had made his controversial revelation: Nature was one immanent substance, a single whole. But then, whither mind and man? Among the first to cast humanity in a new role on Spinoza’s stage were the German Romantics. In the writings of Johann Gottfried Herder, Friedrich Hölderlin, Novalis, Friedrich Schelling, and others, God or Nature became a living force, not fixed but constantly improvising and creating itself.

As this great cosmic mind develops itself out of formless unity, first matter emerges, then creatures, as nature progressively unfolds toward ever more complex beings. Instead of a transcendent and all-creating God, Genesis is reversed: The lower organisms precede the higher.3 In the words of Schelling, who gave these ideas their most forceful articulation, Spinoza’s fixed nature became temporalized as a “dynamic sequence of stages,” a transcendental development of nature’s archetypal potencies, realized exceedingly slowly over cosmic history.4

The Romantic telling culminates with history’s final purpose: humankind. In human consciousness, nature reaches its highest state of organization, coming into awareness of itself. As Schelling says, “It is not that I know but that the universe knows through me.”5 We are one with nature. Yet within it we are also free. The human ability to think, choose, and create for ourselves is our intentional expression of the universe’s creative drive.

Johann Fichte was infamous for his rousing lectures in which he exhorted his students to a life of free will; perhaps Goethe had him in mind when he had his Faust rewrite the Gospel of John: “In the beginning was the act!” These anecdotes, though, understate how the Romantics understood our freedom. These breathtaking passages from Fichte’s humanist apologia The Vocation of Man depict nature, and man’s place in it, as the Romantics saw it:

This life, made manifoldly sensible to mortal eye, flows down through me into all of immeasurable nature. . . . The kinship of spirits flows out into the tenderness of parents and children and siblings, as though souls also were born of one blood, like bodies, and minds were branches and blossoms of the same tree; and from there, in narrower and wider circles, it embraces the whole sentient world.

Through what appears to others as dead mass my eye sees this eternal life and movement in all veins of sensible and spiritual nature; and it sees this life constantly increasing and growing and purifying itself for its own more spiritual self-expression. The universe no longer seems to me that circle returning into itself, that endlessly repeating game, that monster which devours itself so as to give birth to itself again as it already was. For my eyes it has become spiritualized and bears the mark proper to spirit: constant progress to greater perfection in a straight line which goes on to infinity.6

Progress to infinity here does not mean the Enlightenment tradition of the advancement of rational knowledge and the improvement of the human condition. The Romantics were not believers in progress of this kind, and as a matter of fact considered Greco-Roman culture superior to their own. “Infinity” instead refers to humanity’s pure striving, the limitlessness of our potential thought and action.7

Thus the Romantics integrated Spinoza’s monist natural order while freeing humanity from his mechanistic fatalism. Nature has a special place for us after all: In human creativity is to be found the highest expression of nature’s intrinsic productivity. And through humanity, nature becomes “spiritualized.” The high human endeavors of art and philosophy fulfill nature’s ultimate goal to become aware of itself and to direct its own development.

This was an inspiring new role for humanity, unleashing a revolution in our self-understanding. Spinoza had been accused of atheism, of secularizing nature and making a machine out of man. The Romantics redivinized both, made nature a breathing, living ecology, and made humanity not just her finest specimen but the fullest realization of her essence.

To this day, spiritual seekers find it profound to contemplate our identity with the universe, although they are more likely to attribute the notion that we are “the universe experiencing itself” to Alan Watts than to Schelling. And crucially, in envisioning nature as an unfolding whole, the Romantic Naturalphilosophen introduced the motif of evolution that in subsequent centuries would come to characterize the quandary of human meaning.

The rise of the evolutionary story

By the turn of the 19th century, German scientists and Naturalphilosophen had developed a rich conceptual framework. They postulated that a “formative drive” (Bildungstrieb) accounted for the development of an embryo into a complex organism, speculated that environmental pressures drove the “transmutation” of species toward higher beings, and proposed that embryonic development recapitulated the history of life, all leading up to humanity.8

Less than a hundred years after the Romantic heyday, these nascent evolutionary theories were given a scientific hypothesis in the form of a new, controversial publication: Charles Darwin’s Origin of Species. Darwin offered a direct mechanism for the descent of humanity from ancestor species, turning the Bildungstrieb into natural selection. Like the shift from a terracentric to a heliocentric worldview, this marked a transition from anthropocentric grand narratives to ones centered on the process of life as a whole.

Darwin’s theory instantly provoked concern. Christians and naturalists alike expressed caution. Even for scientists like Charles Lyell, a friend of Darwin and pioneer of geological dating, the idea of a simian origin for humans was profoundly uncomfortable. Britain’s leading anatomist, Richard Owen, made increasingly desperate attempts to show a difference in kind, not degree, between humans and animals.9

But the genie was out of the bottle. The human form was not ordained, but evolved. Within a decade, questions about the natural selection of moral and mental faculties among humans — and the possibility of further evolving the human species — could be found in the weekly magazines.10

The evolutionary schema provided the foundation for a new story about humanity’s role in the universe. For centuries humans had already applied selective breeding techniques to improve flowers, fruit, and livestock. With the publication of the Origin, it became impossible not to ask: Might the human race be perfected by the same means?

Officially christened “eugenics” by Darwin’s cousin Francis Galton, clubs dedicated to this aim were everywhere by the end of the 19th century. Eugenics societies were primarily concerned with hereditary intellectual and physical conditions — both with breeding geniuses and with promoting contraception policies for the “unfit” possessors of less desirable traits. Of course, after the horrors of World War II, geneticists and social thinkers were eager to distance themselves from biological racism and utopian projects. Eugenics societies survived, but publicly shifted their focus to medical genetics. The progressive evolutionary principle, however, was carried into a new movement coined by Julian Huxley: transhumanism.

Huxley, the one-time head of the British Eugenics Society, took the eugenic agenda of intentional evolution and elevated it to a role of universal responsibility. Humanity’s purpose is not merely to improve its own stock, but to determine “the future direction of evolution on this earth.” This would be done by developing “native talent” in humankind, but more directly through genetic selection and modification: “deliberate control of the mechanisms of heredity.”11

Eugenics advocates were largely geneticists and early social scientists; the prescient Huxley, by contrast, wanted to make transhumanism into a religious instrument, a new “myth of progress,” in which man’s eugenic and cultural advancement is cast as a microcosm of the evolving whole.12 “‘I believe in transhumanism’: Once there are enough people who can truly say that, the human species will be on the threshold of a new kind of existence [...]”13

Meanwhile, another spiritual evolutionism was forming from a surprising combination of Darwinism and Romanticism. I am not referring here to the humorous episode of Darwinists taken in by fraudulent Spiritualist seances. I am instead speaking of a general effort among thinkers to restate the Romantic vision of creative Nature under the new conditions of the natural sciences.

The first half of the 20th century saw some of its greatest philosophical minds — among them Henri Bergson, Sri Aurobindo, Teilhard de Chardin, Rudolph Steiner, and Alfred North Whitehead — champion their own versions of this modernized Romanticism. This generation took Darwin for granted, accepting deep time, evolution, and the animal origin of man as facts. But they interpreted evolution as the universe’s own ceaseless striving, emphasizing, like Schelling before them, a creatively evolving cosmos in which consciousness is inseparable from matter.

Each had their own take on it. In Creative Evolution, a blowout bestseller in 1907, Bergson explained that the universe’s vitalistic impulse, the élan vital, flows into matter, branching out into evolution and intelligent life. Aurobindo and Teilhard saw consciousness evolving in discrete stages, the human being its leading edge. Regardless of the model, the universe’s productivity is most fully expressed in humanity’s ability to think and act freely.

Darwin had made consciousness a product of evolution. But, these thinkers held, if consciousness has been there from the first, evolving alongside us, then a higher consciousness is a biological inevitability.

Just how could this further evolution be achieved? Bergson thought that the mystic had greater access to the elan vital than any other figure in society. Aurobindo had something similar in mind. In the yogic traditions that formed his background, the yogi was always known to achieve certain supernormal powers. These powers he understood in an explicitly evolutionary fashion, as “a physical working of divine life in the human frame and even the evolution upon earth of something that we may call a divinely human body.”14 Through mystical practice, whether ascetic devotion or Aurobindo’s integral yoga, we can achieve the next stage of the universe’s productive impulse. Like eugenics and transhumanism, this is an evolutionary vision both cosmic and pragmatic.

These thinkers left a large but largely unacknowledged legacy on 20th-century spiritual movements, including the New Age. In particular, they would greatly influence the young Michael Murphy, co-founder of esoteric California retreat center Esalen Institute, where Julian Huxley’s brother Aldous would visit shortly before his death. Indeed, while Julian had coined “transhumanism,” Aldous Huxley’s notion of latent “human potentialities” would inspire at Esalen the Human Potential Movement.15

The Huxley brothers perfectly represent the post-Darwinian split between ideas about humanity’s role in evolution, a split between “life” and “mind.” For Julian, evolution meant a genetic and physical continuation of our species’ development through the use of science — a technological extension of the Romantic vision of humankind. For the perennialist, mystic, and psychedelic enthusiast Aldous, humanity becomes superhumanity by unlocking new realms of consciousness. Both children of the Romantics, these sibling movements each sought to recover human importance, but in quite different ways. Both have become influential in the hothouse of Silicon Valley.

The evolutionary siblings

Welcome to San Francisco in 2026, where I write this essay surrounded on one side by technology optimists and biohackers who have inherited the transhumanist plan of species advancement, and on the other by Northern California spiritual practitioners, who entice me to self-transformation workshops and non-dual awakening. The overlap between these two communities can be surprising; here and there you’ll find a cryonics expert who has tasted states of Buddhist no-self. But generally speaking, these inheritors of the evolutionary story are committed to one or the other philosophy.

Nearly 70 years since Julian Huxley first published on transhumanism, the movement has matured. Huxley’s notebooks were filled with endless lists of “possibilities” for enhanced biochemistry, enhanced humans, enhanced biosocieties and so on;16 today, many of these augmentations have become reality. We have gene therapies that can cure hereditary diseases, we have amino acid injections that could make us live longer, we have in-vitro fertilization for selecting embryos, we have prostheses, treatments, and surgeries that can make us beautiful. The next generation of wonders, such as brain-computer interfaces and miracle longevity drugs, seem to be not too far away.

Partially fulfilling Huxley’s desire for a religion-like institution, transhumanists have settled on at least two core spiritual principles that demarcate the role they envision for humanity. The first principle is a reprisal of Huxley’s belief that evolution is a matter we must take into our own hands. It has been put most eloquently by one of today’s most incisive transhumanist thinkers, Steve Fuller, who advocates for a renewed eugenic project: “Transhumanists should regard Darwin as someone who fell at the final hurdle of the Enlightenment project, at least when it came to the full redemption of humanity’s divine entitlement. . . . Pace Darwin, we cannot simply be capable of adaptively responding to changes in the natural environment. In addition, we must have the courage to adopt the role of Natural Selector.”17 Fuller uses the full weight of Christian theology to make the “theomimetic” aspect of transhumanism explicit: We must take our newfound ability to “play God” most seriously.18

The second principle begins with the transhumanist intuition that we must not be limited by the existing form and function of the human body. This position has been articulated by many, but is stated most famously in Max More’s “Amendment to the Human Constitution.”19 The axiom of morphological freedom, properly put, has a Kantian framing: We have a right to change our own form in whichever way we like, so long as it doesn’t infringe on anyone else. You may put a magnet in your hand, may change your sex, your face, your race, and so on. Thus transhumanists have typically been liberal when it comes to gender reassignment surgery, and in recent years have advocated to remove legal injunctions against personal experimentation with the likes of not-yet-FDA-approved gene therapies. This is a less prescriptive role for humanity, but nevertheless one that recognizably fits in with the modern Western legal tradition’s emphasis on natural human rights. Taken together, these two principles offer a certain vision of the human subject. We are not homo sapiens but homo plasticus, the being that changes its own form. Visionary 1970s transhumanist F.M. Esfandiary makes this explicit in one manifesto (emphasis his): “The more we humans remake our bodies the more human we will grow. We have been pre-human.”20

In contrast to transhumanism, which looks fondly to science fiction books to imagine how technology can improve and transform our lives, the evolutionary mysticism of the Human Potential Movement looks to the past for inspiration, asking: If ancient religious traditions describe saints, mystics, and yogis who possessed superhuman powers, why don’t we?

In his magnum opus The Future of the Body, Michael Murphy provides a taxonomy of extraordinary capacities documented from nearly every religious tradition.21 These latent potentialities range from the common, like synesthesia, to the unusual, such as spontaneous states of ecstasy, to the downright supernormal — clairvoyance, telepathy, and out-of-body experiences. While most traditions disavow the use of powers gained along the path, viewing them as a distraction from God or enlightenment, Murphy sees them as the sign of burgeoning evolution, not unlike the superhero franchise X-Men. Like his inspiration Aurobindo before him, Murphy believed supernormal powers point to the possibility of transforming our human nature. They are the basis for an evolutionary self-transcendence.

The Human Potential Movement, it must be clarified, no longer exists as a singular cultural force. With Esalen now largely a retreat center for the wealthy, its spinout Aurobindian sibling California Institute for Integral Studies having its own identity crisis, and Murphy nearing the end of his long and venerable life, there are vanishingly few people who today would declare themselves advocates of Human Potential.

Still, its influence is felt everywhere in California mysticism. Substantive recent press coverage of the jhanas — states of meditative concentration ranging from MDMA-like bliss to total cessation of consciousness — is just the tip of the iceberg. Northern California, the global home base of transhumanism, is also a hotspot for mystics and mind-body practitioners, many of whom come from lineages that passed through Esalen Institute in the ’60s and ’70s. Here it is possible to find teachers and schools for powers of every variety: energy healing, group field awareness, sexual energy work, blindfolded seeing or “mindsight,” non-duality, kundalini awakening, and many more. Silicon Valley executives who attend psychological training like Hoffman Process or psychedelic retreats are likely to branch out into more esoteric practices.

Esalen had been a home to a consistent set of staff and practitioners who developed an understanding of how practices are or aren’t related, are or aren’t integrated. A book like The Future of the Body, the greatest statement of Human Potential, tied together these lineages into a coherent vision.22 Now this loose collection of practices, from gestalt psychology to tantra, has largely lost the evolutionary framing. In keeping with our time’s emphasis on trauma as a universal source of evil, they are instead viewed as personal and social correctives. If technologists are healed, the thesis seems to be, they will build better, will stop warring with each other about AI alignment, and will renounce their desires for wealth beyond measure and be happy with a mansion in the Oakland hills.

The challenge of AI

Today, a new challenge to humanity rears its head. With the meteoric rise of AI companies, the question of human worth has once again become significant. For white-collar workers and artists, AI already poses a specific personal threat. But it also raises existential anxieties about human displacement writ large. In a recent essay, a mathematician pleads for a pause to AI development and mourns that recent advances in AI mathematics undermine “the story of human discovery and the triumph of the human spirit.”23 The suicidal ideation disclosed by the author is induced not by the prospect of job loss but by the loss of human meaning more broadly. In places outside of Silicon Valley, a Luddite movement disavows the AI project completely, demanding data center bans and a return to human-scale sociability.

Such reactionary responses that impulsively try to protect human sacredness will not be adequate to address the world-historical consequences of this new technology. But how do our two evolutionary humanisms reckon with artificial intelligence?

Transhumanist literature has long fantasized about AI. Yet now that it has arrived, it poses an urgent doctrinal question: Exactly how focused on the human should transhumanism be? AI may be seen as merely another tool to enhance humanity, or alternately, as a new species, one with capacities that greatly exceed our own.

The moderate transhumanism of the former view simply does not possess the resources to deal with a concept as powerful as AI. Peptides, supplements, and cosmetic surgeries do not make us superhuman; they are rapidly becoming table stakes wellness products. What does it matter if we can live longer, work out harder, and think smarter if there is nothing worthwhile left to apply ourselves to? As bizarre as such a transhumanism would be, this position has found a champion in thinker Bryan Johnson, whose doctrine of “Don’t Die” states that as AI takes more and more opportunities off the human plate, just continuing to exist shall be our new ultimate value.24

For those who take the alternate view that AI is a new species and remain committed to transhumanism’s evolutionary mandate, uncomfortable, even antihuman consequences may be drawn: Humans should willingly make way for more complex life forms, even to the extreme point of abandoning human life in favor of a “worthy successor.”25

Dan Faggella, the author of that particular genocidal circumlocution, does not stand alone here. He is joined by a lively cast of misanthropic characters, including Benjamin Bratton and Nick Land.
