1

These are established worries previously explored by Galen Strawson, Kieran Setiya, and me, among others.

item.title: How wheat came to feed the world
item.description: The history of civilization is the history of wheat.
item.content:encoded:
By Thomas Kirk

This article originally appeared in Issue 16: Flourishing. Subscribe to the print magazine by December 18 to receive our upcoming issue, Secrets.

According to Sumerian myth, when the world was young, there was no farming, no cattle, and no weaving. The original gods were forced to live in poverty. To solve this problem they created Ashnan, the goddess of grain, and Lahar, the god of sheep, and sent them to humans to cultivate their gifts.

Together, Ashnan and Lahar furnished the rest of the pantheon with bread, beer, milk, and hides. But the new gods quarreled about which was greater. Enki, the god of wisdom, judged Ashnan the superior, reasoning that without grain there would be no bread, no beer, and, by extension, no cities and no Sumer.

The ancient Sumerians recognized something still true today: The story of wheat is the story of people. Human consumption of wheat is older than cities, older than writing, older than the wheel. In fact, some of the very earliest surviving examples of writing, which, like wheat, originate in the Middle East, aren’t epic poems or religious texts but administrative records of the storage and taxation of grain. Other staple crops dominated in other parts of the world (like rice in East Asia, and maize in the Americas), but it was wheat that fueled the Roman Empire and the Industrial Revolution. Wheat now provides one-fifth of the world’s calories. The fact that it does so is thanks to centuries of human ingenuity and scientific improvement.

Shattering what came before

Six thousand years ago, when the Sumerian civilization was beginning to emerge in what is now Iraq, human consumption of grain was already ancient history. Remains of domesticated wheat from around 10,000 years ago have been found in Anatolia. These leftovers were wild emmer and einkorn (two progenitors of wheat), which looked a lot like the other wild grasses growing around them: a tall stalk topped by a small seed head. They were variably distributed throughout the landscape, and their seeds ripened at different times, so collecting them would have been laborious. Nonetheless, the people of the ancient Levant found the effort worthwhile, as the seeds were calorie-dense and stored well.

By farming wheat, humans unintentionally made it worse but also improved it. Wild wheat had reproduced without human assistance for millions of years. Its seeds, the grains that we eat, are attached to the head of the plant by a thin stalk called a rachis. When the seeds are mature, the rachis shatters, dispersing the seeds on the ground.

This process is essential for wild wheat to reproduce. Human intervention removed this selection pressure, allowing plants that did not shatter to reproduce. Because nonshattering is a recessive trait, nonshattering plants cannot produce shattering offspring.1 As a result, nonshattering plants proliferated, supplanting their wild predecessors. This is how archaeologists observed that domestication was underway.2

Neolithic farmers collected and planted seeds from the heads of plants that remained intact, whereas seeds that had already fallen to the ground were less likely to be harvested or planted. Stores of emmer and einkorn dated as early as 7600 B.C.E. show rough scars, not the smooth tears left by spontaneous shattering, indicating that the natural reproductive process had been interrupted by harvesters. Once the seed-shattering trait had disappeared, wheat was almost completely dependent on humans collecting and planting its seeds to reproduce. In perhaps a thousand years, millions of years of selection for seed shattering had been undone.

On the positive side, yields went up. Grains grew bigger thanks to human cultivation. Naturally, grain size varied, but larger grains were less likely to be blown away or slip out of harvesters’ baskets and were therefore overrepresented in the seeds saved and replanted. On top of that, humans tend to plant seeds deeper than they naturally scatter, and larger seeds are more likely to germinate at greater depths. These processes are thought to have increased grain size by a quarter over the first 500 to 1,000 years of cultivation. By this time, wheat could no longer thrive without help from humans. But the transition to agrarian, sedentary communities enabled by bigger harvests also marked the beginning of our dependence on farming.

Path of yeast resistance

The next important step came just as wheat was beginning to spread to surrounding regions, when it absorbed a whole new set of genes from another species.

One way plants differ from animals is that they can hybridize much more easily, sometimes even happily adding whole new genomes to their own. Long before domestication, emmer wheat had already done this: Wild emmer is a naturally occurring amalgam of a cousin of einkorn and another species known as goat grass (Aegilops speltoides). Emmer is therefore tetraploid, meaning it has four sets of chromosomes.

Emmer and einkorn wheat diffused throughout Anatolia to Cyprus and beyond as farmers migrated out of the Fertile Crescent. Around this time, emmer hybridized again, incorporating the genome of a second species of goat grass (Aegilops tauschii), bringing its chromosome set count to six. This hybridized wheat, which first appears in the archaeological record in northeastern Turkey around 6000 B.C.E., thrived because it had two valuable traits. First, it was free-threshing. Before this, farmers had to pound grains with a mortar and pestle to free them from their tough outer husks, adding a labor-intensive step to every harvest. Second, this new hybrid had higher gluten content, meaning it could form stronger doughs that hold gas, allowing bread to rise. Initially, this saved labor and enabled tastier food. It is now known as bread wheat, or common wheat, and makes up more than 95% of wheat produced today.

Over the next several millennia, cultivation of bread wheat (and agriculture, more or less) spread throughout Europe and Asia. If a plant failed to grow in its new soil or was killed by autumn frosts before reaching maturity, it would be superseded by its better-acclimated relatives. Over thousands of years, incremental changes resulted in countless subtly different local “landrace” populations. Wheat also evolved through further hybridization with closely related plants. This is how we got spelt, which combined the larger grains of bread wheat with the strong shells of emmer, protecting it against the wet and cold and allowing it to thrive further north.

Much of this adaptation was probably incidental, just as early selection for larger seeds and nonbrittle rachises had been. But even in ancient times, careful attention was paid to wheat husbandry and to which varieties thrived in which environments. In 50 B.C.E., the Roman writer Varro advised farmers that “on the threshing-floor the largest and best ears should be placed apart, to furnish the best seed.”3 Long before genetics, farmers understood that good seed begat good crops. This contributed to thousands of years of gradual improvement and specialization.

How to train your einkorn

The Romans may have been intentionally selecting the best plants, but modern scientific wheat breeding began in western Europe in the 19th century. This dramatically sped up yield improvements. A fortuitously large number of early English estate records have survived, meaning we have data for wheat yields starting from before 1275, at which time farmers were producing around 0.6 metric tons per hectare. This was actually worse than the (continental) Romans, who achieved yields up to 1.3 metric tons per hectare.4 Yields remained approximately flat before the 16th century, when they began increasing (and have not stopped).

From the early 1600s through to 1805, yields in Britain almost doubled, increasing from 0.74 in 1604 to 1.26 metric tons per hectare in 1805.5 Deliberate plant selection contributed to this improvement, but intensive selection — that is, aggressively multiplying the very best strains — didn’t really take off until the second half of the 18th century.

Farmers had always wanted to find high-performing seeds, but now they could buy them. Seedsmen emerged, trading hyperadapted local variants like Red Lammas, a strain popular in the 18th century that was known for thriving in chalky soils and making good-quality flour.

Cereals were big business: The original London Corn Exchange6 was built in 1747; the Paris exchange in 1767; Amsterdam had its own Korenbeurs more than a century earlier. From 1765, Britons began importing wheat with the express purpose of finding better varieties, and middlemen living in other countries would send samples of promising grains to contacts in Britain. Yields reflect the results of an increasingly commercialized sector. After stasis for hundreds of years, then steady 2.5% per decade growth in the previous two centuries, yields grew 60% between 1805 and 1865.

In the 19th century, progress was still driven by entrepreneurs, usually curious farmers, rather than scientists. One key innovation, pioneered by Patrick Shirreff in Scotland and John Le Couteur in Jersey, was transitioning from selecting a handful of the best plants to breed from, to selecting the best single individual plant, and multiplying it. They didn’t understand the underlying biology, but the results were clear.

In addition to producing more of the best strains, repeated selection and rebreeding of individuals made the traits of the multiplied strains more consistent from generation to generation. As with shattering seed heads 10,000 years earlier, rebreeding meant undesirable genetic variants were eliminated from the population. Early breeders called this “breeding true,” and though the genetic basis for it was not yet understood, it was important to farmers, who prefer more consistent and predictable crops.

Another important development was the intentional crossing of two plants to create a hybrid. A wheat plant can self-pollinate because it contains both male and female reproductive organs, fertilizing its ovules with its own pollen. The overwhelming majority of wheat plants are produced in this way, and therefore have just one parent, which acts genetically as both mother and father. This process doesn’t produce clones initially because each pollen grain or ovule, even from the same individual, is genetically distinct. But it does result in offspring with extremely limited genetic diversity, which diminishes even further with each successive generation of self-breeding.7

But sometimes cross-pollination produces plants that come from two parents rather than one. In nature this occurs randomly, but plant breeders deliberately take pollen from one plant and use it to fertilize the ovule of another. Shirreff was a pioneer of this technique, too. The best offspring resulting from these crosses would outperform both parents on some key traits. These high-performing varieties would then be multiplied and the seed sold to farmers.

These techniques were adopted throughout Europe, where the Vilmorin Seed Company in France and the Swedish Seed Association in Sweden were among the first to institutionalize cereal breeding. In 1884, The Technology of Bread-Making identified as many as 65 wheat varieties, local and imported, available in English grain markets.

Before the Industrial Revolution, Britain was a largely agricultural nation. But by the end of the 19th century, the population had increased more than sevenfold from about 4 million people in 1600 to 30 million in 1900, and only a tenth of workers were employed in agriculture. This would have been impossible without improvements in agricultural yields. The “dark satanic mills” of the Industrial Revolution needed wheat just as much as they needed coal and child labor.

Limited yields?

The pace of improvement increased as researchers began to understand more about genetics and evolution. The discoveries of Darwin (natural selection) and Mendel (the inheritance of simple genetic traits, like seed shattering) were essential to understanding why and how techniques applied over the previous centuries had worked. Also critical were contributions of Wilhelm Johannsen, who untangled how much traits were shaped by genes as opposed to the environment, and Ronald Fisher, the “father of modern statistics,” who figured out the underlying maths. Fisher also showed how continuous traits like height could be determined by the cumulative effect of many individual genes. These insights, around 100 years ago, led to the development and widespread adoption of statistical tools to identify the best seed varieties and to predict how their offspring would perform.

Breeders generated a vast array of new varieties for testing through a combination of exploration and crossing. Exploration, which was often sponsored by the state, meant collecting seeds from the many unique wheat varieties that had proliferated across the earth since the dawn of time. Britain’s Watkins Landrace Wheat Collection, for example, created in the 1930s, acquired more than 800 wheat cultivars from 32 countries, which could be crossed to create more than 300,000 new hybrid varieties. The USDA had the largest program. Using genetic material from these collections, nurseries would generate crosses for initial testing, multiplying the seeds until there were enough to carry out trials. Trials across several locations allowed researchers to distinguish the effects of genes and environment.

But there were still constraints holding back wheat yields. One was wheat rust, a fungal disease that leaves a characteristic orange-brown powdery residue on plants before shriveling and killing them. Ancient writers knew about this disease: The Romans even had a yearly festival, the Robigalia, in which they performed rituals meant to keep it at bay. In the worst-affected years of the mid-20th century, wheat rust was killing off nearly 20% of American wheat. Breeding programs developed resistant varieties, but any respite was short-lived as the fungus would quickly evolve a new line of attack.

Another was wheat plants “lodging,” or falling over under their own weight. Fertilizer had become much cheaper thanks to the Haber-Bosch process for making ammonia from nitrogen gas, developed in 1909. But its usefulness for improving wheat production was limited because although fertilizer could in theory make the plants grow larger than before, applying it would often make the stems collapse, making the wheat unharvestable.

At the time, these problems seemed to show that there were fundamental trade-offs limiting yields. It was assumed that further improvements would be incremental. This fueled worry that there would soon be insufficient food for the growing global population; biologist Paul Ehrlich predicted in 1968 that “in the 1970s hundreds of millions of people will starve to death.”

The Green Revolution

These gloomy forecasts turned out to be dead wrong. Between 1950 and 1990, wheat yields in many countries — rich and poor — doubled, as did the yields of other crops: the fastest improvement to farming efficiency ever seen. This explosive growth, enabled by advances in breeding together with mechanization and the wider adoption of fertilizer, is referred to as the “Green Revolution.” Norman Borlaug, an American agronomist often called the father of the Green Revolution, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for his work. In 2009 the director of the World Food Programme said that Borlaug “saved more lives than any man in human history.”

Borlaug didn’t discover anything new — he just implemented existing techniques better than anyone had before. In 1944, he joined the Mexican Agriculture Program (an initiative founded and funded by the Rockefeller Foundation) under which he produced about 6,000 new crosses over a decade, a huge quantity at a time when most breeders managed fewer than 200 per year. This quantity was essential to generating the high-performing outliers that could become popular new varieties. It is even more important when two traits you want (like yield and gluten content) are negatively correlated: The more varieties you test, the likelier you are to find one that bucks the trend, performing well on both.

Rather than approaching yield directly, the program focused on two main limiting factors: wheat rust and lodging. The intensive program of crossing and selecting made it possible to develop varieties that carried several forms of resistance to rust at once, and crossbreeding with Japanese “dwarf” wheat varieties, which were shorter and more robust, produced plants that could be juiced up with fertilizer without collapsing. By the 1960s, Borlaug had produced wheat varieties that had it all: resistance to lodging, multiple resistance to wheat rust, and high yields.

One way this breeding program differed from previous ones was that it was split between two separate regions. The original purpose of this was to squeeze two growing seasons into one year, halving the time it took to produce a new generation. After producing the first generation of offspring in the Toluca highlands, west of Mexico City, Borlaug moved the plants north to the lower-altitude Yaqui Valley, then produced the second generation in time to move back south for the following year. In these stages, selection was crude: Only varieties that failed to germinate or were affected by rust were culled. But later stages of the breeding program included yield trials and statistical selection methods.

Alternating between two regions had another, perhaps serendipitous, benefit.8 By advancing candidates that survived in both locations, Borlaug had selected those that could perform well across different environments. Selection for photoperiod-insensitive seeds (those able to mature in both despite differing daylight exposure) meant that varieties developed in Mexico might be successfully grown in other countries, and therefore could be shared across the world. Not all plants, and certainly not all wheat, can be photoperiod insensitive, but varieties tested by the Mexican Agriculture Program were, which may explain why wheat was the first crop to flourish in the Green Revolution. Maize, for example, is so sensitive that breeders operate semi-independent breeding programs for different latitudes.

If Ehrlich was aware of this work when he predicted mass starvation in 1968, he cannot have known its significance. In the mid-1960s, India and Pakistan began importing Borlaug’s new wheat varieties. One descendant of these imported wheats (called Kalyan Sona or “golden savior”) performed extremely well and became one of the most commonly planted varieties in the region. From 1965 to 1975, wheat yields in India and Pakistan nearly doubled;9 production increased so much and so quickly that there were shortages of labor for harvest. Over time, other less developed countries followed a similar path.

Precision breeding

The next stage of plant breeding was identifying specific genes for the precise properties that farmers wanted. The problem was that genotyping and genome sequencing were expensive and slow. The first genome was sequenced in 1977, but it belonged to a bacteriophage (a virus that infects bacteria) with a genome nearly a million times smaller than a human’s. Sequencing the first human genome cost somewhere between $300 million and $3 billion, and was achieved much later. And this was just a diploid human genome. Wheat has a genome five times larger than that, partly because of its three hybridized subgenomes.

Breeders came up with a comparatively quick and dirty solution: marker-assisted selection. Instead of tracking genes directly, they used much cruder tests to find genetic features (“markers”) that correlated with given traits. One technique was restriction fragment length polymorphism analysis, in which scientists use enzymes to chop DNA into pieces and then literally measure how long the resulting fragments are by how quickly they are pulled through gel by an electric current. While breeders would not know which genes were responsible for traits, they would know that a trait was correlated with a particular pattern of fragment lengths when cut with a particular enzyme.

Despite the crudeness of the method, it still worked for some traits, especially simple ones like rust resistance, which is often controlled by one or two genes. This allowed farmers and breeders to work out whether a variety was going to be good without going through a whole season of growing, as Norman Borlaug had to. This marker-assisted selection for many crops became routine in the 1990s. Field trials remained important, but most strains were filtered out at the marker identification stage, and few ever made it to the field. At the beginning of the decade, only a few hundred markers were known, but by the end, this had expanded to thousands.

Early marker-assisted selection was of limited use for traits like yield, which are influenced by thousands of genes. But we are no longer restricted to looking at a small number of genetic markers. DNA sequencing costs have decreased by a factor of 100,000 since 2000. Now breeders will often use “genomic selection”: essentially, using the entire genome as a marker and letting statistical software predict which genomes are associated with different traits. Genomic selection can tell us if 500 different genes each contribute 0.2% to a trait where traditional marker-assisted selection would have been useless.

This has revolutionized the process of plant breeding — if not the outcome.10 Global crop yields continue to increase at a steady rate, reflecting the fact that progress is getting harder to come by. We can now use the same genetic prediction tools for complex traits, like yield, grain quality, and drought tolerance, that we once did for simple ones. At the time Norman Borlaug was working, it took months or years and thousands of wheat plants to evaluate a new variety’s performance. Today, it can take just days to germinate a seedling and make predictions based on a small leaf sample.

Our daily bread

Pessimists would say that wheat domesticated us, that we have spent thousands of years in backbreaking labor serving its reproductive ends. Optimists would argue our coevolution has benefited humanity far more, liberating us from a state of subsistence and creating a caloric surplus to sustain the lives of billions.

The human species used to live hand to mouth: Virtually all our labor was devoted to growing and harvesting food to fend off starvation. Now, in most developed countries, only a tiny fraction of the population works in agriculture. Wheat’s astonishing success is a crucial part of this change. It is the most widely grown crop on earth, covering 1.5% of the planet’s total land area, and is responsible for one-fifth of the world’s calorie intake. But the amount of labor required to produce those calories has decreased enormously. Since 1900, despite the world’s population increasing more than fourfold, the price of wheat is roughly a quarter of what it was.

That transformation is the result of sustained, incremental improvement to yield, to pathogen resistance, to ease of harvest, to taste, to gluten content, and much more. The advancements came from early farmers unknowingly favoring larger seeds; from finicky varieties that couldn’t handle frost, drought, and other hardships being killed off by the elements; and from breeders making active choices about what traits they wanted to cultivate, increasingly backed by the might of modern science. Today, we can sequence wheat’s entire genome and select for exactly the traits we want. Advances in breeding mean that similar stories can be told for every other major crop and farm animal. Each of us now enjoys the fruits of these advances at every mealtime.

A lot has changed since the first wheat was farmed in the Fertile Crescent. But Enki is just as correct now as he was thousands of years ago: We would have no Sumer without grain.

Thomas Kirk is a plant and animal breeding program consultant at AbacuSio.

This article originally appeared in Issue 16: Flourishing. Subscribe to the print magazine by December 18 to receive our upcoming issue, Secrets.

1

Remember Punnett squares? Two shattering parents (Ss) will produce 75% shattering offspring (25% homozygous and 50% heterozygous) and 25% nonshattering (ss), but two nonshattering parents will produce 100% nonshattering offspring.

2

A lower percentage of stored grain with shattered rachises indicates cultivation had been going on for longer.

3

Modern breeding programs work exactly the same way: Identify the best plants, use them to produce the next generation, and repeat.

4

Romans measured yield as ratios of harvested grain to seed sown, both measured by volume. Estimates range from 4-to-1 to 10-to-1. Seed was typically planted at five modii per iugerum, or about 133 kilograms per hectare; therefore yields would have been from 0.5 to 1.3 metric tons per hectare.

5

Farmers began to grow winter fodder, such as turnips, to feed animals over winter. This allowed them to keep more of them. More animals meant more manure, which increased soil nitrogen and helped improve yields.

6

At the time, “corn” was a catchall term for all cereal crops, including barley and oats as well as wheat.

7

Each generation, the proportion of heterozygous recessive pairs (like the nonshattering plants with the ss gene) increases, slowly reducing the genetic variation existing within the plant (ss*ss = 100% ss).

8

Borlaug claimed this was intentional, but most other accounts disagree.

9

In 59 years from 1965 to 2024, wheat yield in India and Pakistan increased by 290% and 280%, respectively. Much faster than France (87%) and Germany (144%) from 1850 to 1911.

10

Genomics has revolutionized the rate of genetic progress in dairy cattle, however, through a similar mechanism to plants: speeding up breeding by reducing the generation interval.

item.title: The most important number in AI
item.description: A deep dive into the Epoch Capabilities Index.
item.content:encoded:
By Clara Collier

If your timeline is anything like mine, you’re seeing a lot of people panicking about lines on graphs. More often than not, they’re lines on one particular graph: the Epoch Capabilities Index. The ECI, developed by Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization, has become our most reliable single measure of AI progress. While everyone else is debating how fast it’s increasing and what it tells us about an intelligence explosion or the state of the American-Chinese capabilities gap, I wanted to step back and understand how it’s made.

Alexander Barry is a researcher at Epoch who helps develop the ECI. Florian Brand works on open models at Prime Intellect and previously contracted for Epoch. We discuss:

  • How the ECI is constructed

  • The challenges of benchmark selection

  • Whether it even makes sense to talk about “model IQ”

  • Whether static benchmarks will stay relevant as models get better

…and much more.


—Clara Collier

Clara Collier: Alexander, do you want to start by explaining the ECI?

Alexander Barry: We built it to give a single number that summarizes how well AI models do on benchmarks. It’s built using a relatively simple statistical model that takes in a bunch of benchmark results and outputs a single capability number, or ECI score, for each model.

One notable thing about it is that we designed it to be continuously updatable. Even as individual benchmarks saturate or drop out and new benchmarks get introduced, you can just add the new ones and still get results on one scale. So you can look at trends going back years and forecast things for future models.

Clara: My understanding is that it’s based on item response theory, so it assumes there’s a single quantity that’s correlated across all of a model’s benchmark scores. That’s related to the methodology used for IQ tests in humans, which assumes that all of the subtasks are measuring the same fundamental quality of general intelligence. Is that assumption warranted for current AI models?

Alexander: It’s worth saying that it clearly is an assumption, and it’s clearly not literally true. AI models do have relative strengths and weaknesses to some degree. You might notice that a model happens to be a bit better at math benchmarks than at some other type of benchmark.

But — and this is a purely empirical result — I do think it’s very, very close to being true. Normally, if you get a new frontier flagship model, it’s probably better on pretty much every benchmark than a model from six months ago. The gaps between different ability dimensions aren’t so big that they make up for much of that progress. We do have some things that try to track this more directly — domain-specific versions that look just at math or just at software engineering. You do get some differences, but it’s normally a few ECI points, maybe three to five at the high end. I know these numbers are all kind of meaningless on their own, but we see models normally increase by about 15 points a year.

Clara: So when people say models are jagged, they often mean that models have spiky, weird capability distributions relative to humans. But they’re not jagged relative to each other.

Alexander: Yes, that’s a very good point. This is all about looking only at AI models.

Clara: Why did you choose this approach for the ECI, as opposed to other metrics people have used, like METR’s time horizon approach, which looks at the length of tasks that models are able to complete at a certain level of accuracy?

Alexander: I have a lot of positive things to say about time horizons, and I should note that I’ve worked on it in various capacities, so I might be biased. But I think the real advantage of the ECI approach is that all you need is benchmark results. The model learns how to interpret each benchmark: how difficult it is and what different results mean. With time horizons, METR had to invest large amounts of effort into collecting human baseline times for all the tasks. That’s an extremely valuable thing to do, but it’s very costly in time and money. And for longer tasks, it might get completely impractical.

To some degree, I also think the ECI approach captures what humans actually do. Say a new model comes out with a bunch of benchmark results, and you’re trying to figure out what they mean about how good the model is. You see it scored really highly on some math benchmark. You might think: If the score was already at 95%, then going to 97% is actually pretty good, because it can only go up to 100. So that’s a big jump — you’re adjusting for the shape of the scale. Or some other benchmark has gone from 0 to 50% to 70% quickly, and you think, wow, that benchmark is changing really fast. So if something new comes along and gets 90, that’s still an improvement, but it’s probably not a crazy one.

In some sense, the ECI approach just formalizes all of those intuitions into a pretty simple mathematical model, along with a few other things, like whether there’s some maximum achievable performance.

Digging deeper into benchmark selection

Clara: Now I want to talk about criticisms of the ECI and how you calculate it. Florian, do you want to start?

Florian Brand: I think, in general, the methodology is hard to criticize.

The beauty of a single index is that it’s super easy to understand. But even though the mathematical model is somewhat simple, it’s hard for people who aren’t deep into these things to understand how it’s calculated and how things relate to each other. I also think continuous numbers are harder for humans to put into context. If I have a benchmark score with 100 as the maximum — which is also a requirement for benchmarks to be included in the ECI at all — we know that a score of 50 means there’s still a lot of room for improvement on that selection of tasks. The ECI is unbounded. It’s very hard to say, “All right, this is the current state of things,” or, “Here’s how an individual benchmark influences a model’s result,” because everything gets thrown into the mathematical model and you get a score out.

Clara: If I had to condense that: The mathematical model is simple, but it still encodes a lot of ultimately subjective decisions about what benchmarks to include and how to weight them. And it’s hard to understand what an ECI number means without being in the weeds of all those decisions.

Florian: I would mostly agree, except that the weighting is not subjective. That’s the mathematical model. But benchmark selection very much is a subjective decision. If you include or exclude certain scores, you can push the model’s results in a different direction.

Clara: So let’s talk about how you choose benchmarks.

Alexander: In theory, the standard is anything that measures capabilities. So it’s not “What color does the model like?” — or important things like whether the model is aligned. We don’t consider those part of a capabilities index. It’s about what models can do.

The other, more subjective element is benchmark quality. And I think I’ll get a lot of agreement on this: There are a lot of very flawed AI benchmarks out there. I think the ECI is very robust in a lot of ways to different modeling assumptions. Something it’s not robust to is benchmarks that saturate at some ceiling below 100% when you don’t know that in advance. It’s fine if you know you can only score 50% on a benchmark; then you can incorporate that. But if it seems like you should be able to score 100%, and then everything only gets 65, that can really screw up your ECI estimates.

So a lot of our decisions come down to saying, “We only want to add benchmarks where we feel pretty confident that either the ceiling is 100% or we know what the ceiling is.” Unfortunately, that’s turned out to be a much harsher criterion than we might have hoped, at least when we introduced the ECI around the start of this year.

People sometimes reasonably say, “This benchmark seems cool. Why don’t you add it?” And unfortunately, lots of benchmarks that seem cool end up having problems that you only run into later. We’ve reasonably frequently taken out benchmarks that we added because they seemed high quality, and then later looked into more closely, both through our own benchmark review program and because other people look at benchmark quality too. Sometimes when we take something out, we notice that it was biasing the results.

Clara: Florian, do you have any specific examples where benchmark selection decisions have led to meaningful reweighting between different models?

Florian: One example is world-knowledge benchmarks. I think the benchmark SimpleQA, which tests factual recuall, is still part of the current selection. That’s a subjective decision, and because it is subjective, all sides are very defensible.

Historically, open models — and I’m a huge proponent of open models — perform rather badly on this benchmark. There are certain labs that care more about encoding world knowledge into the model, so they train bigger models that hold all these obscure facts in their weights. And there’s another school of thought that says, “Everyone is using agents anyway. If the model needs some world knowledge, it will just do 15 searches and get the same result.” That’s also a valid position. But including this benchmark, or this category of benchmarks, influences the ECI. And because it’s one of the benchmarks that differentiates model capabilities, or training choices, really well, it has a big impact on the overall score.

Alexander: I’d be interested in exactly how big the impact is. It used to be bigger.

Florian: It has shrunk a lot. But this is one of the examples where you have implicit weighting by choosing these things. On the other hand, the very valid pushback is that if you have a single index and you have to choose and reweight benchmarks yourself, you introduce even more subjectivity than if you just say, “All right, this is a category or benchmark we think is important. Throw it in.”

Alexander: As much as the entire premise is that you can explain everything very well with one dimension, this knowledge-encoded-in-the-weights thing actually is a bit distinct, because you can really see model size having an influence on it. As a recent example, we’ve got Fable 5.1, and then Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku 5.5. People often find that the smaller recent Anthropic models are surprisingly performant on a bunch of things, but you really notice their size on these knowledge benchmarks. They just very straightforwardly perform worse. So this does have an effect on the weighting. If we constructed an ECI from 50 knowledge benchmarks and 10 other benchmarks, that would definitely change things. Currently, I think SimpleQA Verified is one of the only ones in there. There might be a few others.

One thing is just that we have a lot more insight into the quality of the benchmarks we develop and run at Epoch. I’m not sure there’s ever been a case where we developed one and then decided it wasn’t good enough to put in — normally we’d try to improve it. And we run them very systematically. So there are a lot of Epoch-run benchmark results in there, although there are also lots of external benchmarks. Historically, Epoch made a lot of math benchmarks. We’ve expanded beyond that now, but it does mean there’s a decently large number of math benchmarks.

Clara: I remember there was a debate when Kimi K3 came out about how much of the gap between Kimi K3 and Western models was due to an Epoch-developed benchmark, FrontierMath performance.

Alexander: I’d say we give K3 a pretty high score. And I’d say that very often — with any lab release, really, but particularly with some of the ones from Chinese labs — the benchmarks they choose to highlight paint the model in the best possible light. So there will often be a difference between the impression you get from those and the impression you get from a more generic, unselected set of benchmarks. But yes, there absolutely are choices. One thing we do to allow for this is that, as I said, we have the math ECI and the software engineering ECI, and also the ability to make custom ones, where you pick any subset of the benchmarks we currently include and calculate it with those — since we do have the data. So if you’re like, “I don’t like how much influence SimpleQA has,” you can say, “Show me without SimpleQA.” That’s a totally valid choice. We’re not claiming this is the one true way to do this.

Florian: I think that’s really important, and it also plays back into jaggedness. I mainly code and run experiments with models. I don’t really care about math performance or world knowledge. The things I care about are things like the software engineering ECI, which more closely tracks my experience, and the gap between open and closed models in those areas is much smaller. If you look more broadly, open models are definitely somewhat better on some benchmarks than in real-world performance. But in certain spiky domains, you can definitely see that they’re closer to the closed models.

Clara: Does this challenge the unidimensionality thesis? If the whole idea is that all of these capabilities should be broadly correlated, is it a problem if you have open models that are just as performant on programming tasks but less good at computer use or math or other domains?

Alexander: As I said at the start, the unidimensional thing is not true. It’s a pretty good approximation. If it were literally exactly true, all of these separate sub-indices would be exactly the same. They don’t match exactly; there are some differences.

In particular, I think Kimi K3 does better by two or three ECI points on the software engineering ECI than on the general one. Amusingly, either way, it’s basically equivalent to Opus 4.8, and Opus 4.8 also does better on the software engineering one. That seems very impressive to me. People might differ in how impressive they expect open models to be, but I’m like, man, if you’re as good as Opus 4.8, that’s a very good model. So you’re absolutely right that this is a way the thesis isn’t completely true. But I still think it’s notable that these things are normally very close. The deviations aren’t that big.

The status quo

Clara: So what does an ECI score mean? What’s a recent ECI number? Where are they at now?

Alexander: Around 169.

Clara: 169. Thank you. Commentators can get very exercised about 169 versus 165 versus 172. How do you think about what these numbers are grounded in? What’s the sanity check here? And how do you interpret the scale — how much does a two- or three-point gap “matter”?

Alexander: The numbers are arbitrary, so the way the ECI is defined is that Claude 3.5 Sonnet — the original, not the new one — is 130, and GPT-5 is 150. That’s just set by definition. So a 20-point gap is the gap between Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-5. We’re presumably about to get to an ECI of 170, which is that much again above GPT-5.

On some level that’s a bit like, “Well, what does that mean?” But that’s true of any attempt to put capabilities on a scale. When the ECI launched, people very rightly asked what the number meant. Particularly at the time, when METR time horizons were still the main thing being reported, people would say, “Well, I know what two hours means. I’ve experienced hours of working. But I don’t know what 155 is.”

I think people have gotten more used to these numbers over time; you get a sense. And we can say things like: Since reasoning models came out, there’s been a pretty consistent trend of about 15 to 18 points per year. So if a new model came out that was 10 points higher than the previous frontier model, we’d be like, wow, that’s a giant increase — more than six months of the progress we’d expect. We’d be able to make a big deal about that, and you’d really see it on the trend chart.

It’s clearly better if you can have a scale that’s meaningful in and of itself. So it’s clearly a weakness of the ECI that it’s on an abstract scale. But it’s not completely meaningless. It does have this definition.

Trying to disagree

Clara: This is so friendly. Let’s get to some real disagreements. What are your biggest problems with how the ECI is used, how it’s reported, the impact it has on discourse? I’m sure we can find something.

Florian: Again, the theoretical points are valid, and there are a few things to attack there. But if we want to get into disagreements, it would be a lot of examples of “this particular thing, and this particular thing.”

Clara: I think that’s great. I love specifics.

Florian: That means we have to dive into the details, and those are also easier to fix. But one example that’s somewhat systematic — it’s about the ECI as Epoch implements it, rather than the methodology — is that you’re mixing your own runs with model-developer-reported runs and with third-party runs.

The thing I’m seeing more and more, the more I look into benchmarks, is that no two organizations run the same benchmark the same way — even something as standardized as Terminal-Bench, which measures performance on realistic problems in computer terminal environments. Every time I tried to replicate a score, I was like, “Why is their score so much higher than mine?” Then I’d dive super deep into the system card, which sometimes says these things, or into the setup files, if they exist, and I’d find the one or two changes that have a huge impact.

For Terminal-Bench, for example, it’s very important how you set the wall-clock time. Terminal-Bench 4 solves a lot of this, or at least sets a higher wall-clock limit. But basically, the benchmark creators built the benchmark saying, “All right, there’s a limit, and we expect the models to solve these tasks within it.” That also means you’re measuring things like your latency to the model provider. So everyone kind of agreed that time limits aren’t really useful for measuring capabilities and quietly dropped them — but didn’t say so.

There are a lot of other cases like this. ExploitBench has official numbers from its creators, Anthropic has its own implementation, and OpenAI also has its own implementation. So you can’t compare any of these numbers. ExploitBench in particular has three different setups in the Cyber ECI. I know there’s a reason for that, but for standardized benchmarks, everyone just does whatever. And if—

Alexander: Can I jump in?

Florian: Yeah, sure.

Alexander: I’m sabotaging your attempt to get to disagreements, because I in fact agree completely. This is why we almost never have developer-reported scores in the ECI. The only exception, I think, is from when it was originally set up: For some of the older models and older benchmarks, the norm back then was that you’d run your model on a bunch of stuff and report it, so some of those numbers came from developers. Anything modern is either run by Epoch or run independently by third parties. We actually had a fun case when xAI acquired Cursor: We took out CursorBench, because we were like, “Okay, you’re no longer a third party.”

And as you know, the Cyber ECI is a special case, because it’s just very, very hard to get third-party cyber results. There are very few. So in that case we did have to lower our standards, but we put a lot of effort into trying to adjust for it, because it is a giant headache. In general, though, systematically across the ECI, we don’t ever just take reports from model cards. We only get things from official leaderboards. So I’m afraid we agree.

Florian: Then my pushback — and this has been a lot of my work, both now and when I was contracting for Epoch — is that a lot of benchmarks make design decisions that don’t elicit model capabilities well enough. There’s also no standardization, no “Here’s how everyone does these things.” So everyone is pushing the models in whatever direction they think is good. That means that across different benchmarks, it’s hard to say whether model capabilities are elicited correctly.

To give a more concrete example, it also means that some benchmarks are nicer than others to models that reward-hack or cheat. That’s a problem we’ve discovered more and more, and we don’t really know how to deal with it. It applies to things like Terminal-Bench and OfficeQA and other benchmarks. A lot of third-party evaluations are run with web access, some very deliberately. We’ve done runs on OfficeQA, which is a document-search benchmark that also has some web-search components.

Some models, like DeepSeek V4, just went to the web, found solutions to the benchmark online, and used those, instead of doing web searches for the intended tasks. That means the official score — if you run it the way the benchmark maker intended — is kind of flawed, because the model just did that. Closed models like GPT didn’t do this; they didn’t cheat on these tasks.

That puts everyone in a kind of weird position, because there’s no standard for how to deal with this. It also applies to Terminal-Bench, where some models just look up the solution online, or find ways that aren’t intended. So what do you do with those scores? If you run everything yourself, you can enforce certain rules and be opinionated. But then you’re no longer reporting OfficeQA or Terminal-Bench; you’re reporting your opinion on those benchmarks. And that’s super weird right now.

Alexander: I’d respond on a couple of fronts. The first quick thing is that this falls under the benchmark-quality question: If a benchmark is very susceptible to reward hacking, we’d treat that as a reason not to put it in the ECI. And as an aside, I enjoyed your recent blog post looking at these issues.

The broader point this raises — and it’s a choice we make for the ECI that’s worth discussing — is that we don’t have ECI per dollar. In general, the approach we take for the ECI is to have models run with the maximum elicitation that fits within how each benchmark is set up.

For the benchmarks we run ourselves, we’re normally much more on the side of asking: for any reasonable cost, what’s the maximum performance you can get? But that’s a choice, and some benchmarks are set up to give models substantially fewer resources. WeirdML v2 is in the ECI, and the way it’s set up, models get five attempts at something. It’s quite limited, and it’s not an agentic setup. When the benchmark’s creator looked at giving models an agentic setup, he found they did substantially better. And that probably would have affected different models differently.

Florian: I do think elicitation is a huge thing that’s overlooked in a lot of benchmarks. I see a trend toward stacking a lot of things on top just to be adversarial against the model. One of the results from MirrorCode is that if I sit down and give the model a lot of things that help it — without spoiling the solution, obviously — the models can do a lot, and they can run for weeks. Then a bunch of other benchmarks that came out around that time, or later, basically had the same setup and confirmed that yes, that’s possible. And the more you look into it, the more you see that they made one choice that was somewhat adversarial against the model, then stacked another thing on top, and another thing on top, and that depressed the overall score.

That matters especially for open versus closed models. Open models are weaker. But if you really push them — give them a ton of resources, prompt them a bit more elaborately, and use them in a harness that elicits their capabilities — the gap becomes narrower than a lot of benchmarks suggest.

Alexander: That’s one element of benchmark elicitation: Do you set budgets by tokens, by time, or by dollars? Obviously, if you have open models that are much cheaper, giving them dollar budgets will often make them look much better, because they’ll be able to spend loads of tokens. That might actually match people’s real use case, if people are happy to let it sit and run for ages.

Florian: In the end, you don’t spend tokens. You spend dollars.

Alexander: Yes, but you do spend time — I guess that’s the fair counterpoint.

Florian: But time is always weird. Especially with open models, I can set up a deployment that’s super fast and serves the model quickly, and that shouldn’t be a confounder for the benchmark score. There are cases where open models just spend tokens and tokens on tool calls, and the time difference looks huge. You can manipulate all these things. You can run GPT in its normal setup, or use ultra-fast mode, and that shouldn’t change the score in terms of raw capabilities.

Alexander: I agree. In practice, it’s an unfortunate reality of actually running benchmarks. You’re like, “Man, it would take DeepSeek V4.1 Flash a month to spend all its tokens on this thing, and I don’t want to let it run that long.” But yes, I agree. Maybe we’ve gotten a bit lost in a fun discussion about running benchmarks.

The end of benchmarks?

Clara: I do want to talk about another, related issue, which is that people have been declaring the end of benchmarks for, what, two years now? Static benchmarks are over; they can’t capture what matters; they’re getting saturated. What’s your perspective on how good benchmarks fundamentally are, how good they can be, and whether we’re running out?

Alexander: I’m going to start by having another exciting agreement with Florian. He made a tweet the other day about something I’d also been thinking. I think it’s basically the case that for math and software engineering, it’s no longer possible to make benchmarks of tasks we know a human could do that the models can’t do — at least if you’re measuring real functional capabilities, like “Can they prove this result or find this number?” or “Can they write code that achieves this well-specified goal?” You might still say their papers are horrible, or you don’t like the style of their code. But it works.

That puts us in a bit of a bind for making more benchmarks. For math, the new done thing — which others are doing as well — is to take a bunch of unsolved conjectures, make a big list, try to solve them, and say, “Oh, great, it’s solved five out of 60 of those.” That’s a benchmark, I guess.

Clara: Is FrontierMath formally saturated yet?

Alexander: We keep making new FrontierMath somethings. We had Tiers 1 through 3 and then Tier 4, which were conventional benchmarks: very, very difficult math problems that we got mathematicians to create, but which do have an answer, and we know what it is. Originally, it turned out 40% of the questions were wrong, but then we fixed that, so now it’s fine. Those are now completely saturated — as of GPT-6 Astra, it got very close to 100%.

So now we have new ones. There’s FrontierMath: Open Problems, which is a big collection of very notable open problems. And there’s FrontierMath: Erdős, a curated sample of 68 of the most difficult and notable Erdős problems that were open as of August, all formalized in Lean. We deliberately gave models an offline setup, where we downloaded all the material we thought they could need as of that time. So at least until pretraining catches up, we can run it like a benchmark.

The issue with those is that we don’t really know what the maximum achievable score is. It might be that some of them are just unprovable. That’s a thing about math results: they can be independent of the axioms, and that fact can be unprovable too. So you can never show anything about it. It’s the same with software engineering tasks. We can keep making tasks like “Optimize this kernel and make it really fast,” but once models are doing better than any human has ever done, we don’t know what the limit on performance is. Those difficulties play into building an index like the ECI in particular, because you have to have some sense of how difficult it is to go from one score on a benchmark to another. So I think we’re getting into a difficult regime.

Clara: I want to talk about the ECI and the idea of model benchmarking going forward. Right now, it seems like we have this number that’s kind of like model IQ. I had a very funny conversation with one of your colleagues, who was saying that doing this work has made her kind of an IQ skeptic, because measuring this is so much simpler and easier for models than for humans — and it’s still pretty hard for models. So what do we do going forward? Do you think the ECI is going to break? What are your plans for handling this?

Alexander: I specifically raised math and software engineering because those are areas where models are exceptionally strong compared to humans. There are still plenty of areas where they’re not that strong. We can make something like VideoGameBench, and they do okay. But if the task is beating Call of Duty or something — a first-person game where you have to control things quickly in real time — they’re really not that good at that yet. So it’s not the case that we currently can’t make any hard tasks.

Clara: It seems like Astra is comparatively much better at math than at video games. It’s way better at math than almost any human, and it’s worse at video games than most humans. But it made a big step up in math, and also a big step up in video games. They’re still correlated. Do you think that’s going to keep being the case with future models?

Relatedly, right now, it’s hard to distinguish between two possibilities. One is that there’s a true underlying model g that comes out of the training process holistically. The other is that we have a very rich and sophisticated range of specific post-training environments for all of these things, and bigger models are also post-trained more, on more things, so they’re going to correlate for that reason. But that correlation would be kind of superficial. You can imagine changing the post-training mix, and then these things come apart.

Alexander: We do sometimes try quite hard to build benchmarks where we’re like, “There’s no way anyone tried to train on anything even particularly like this.” And we still see big improvements.

One thing that’s shaped my thinking on this recently — it’ll be out by the time this is published — is a new endurance reasoning benchmark we made. It’s just very, very simple but very, very long problems, like adding two 50,000-digit numbers together, where you can scale the number of digits, or calculating the determinant of a 20-by-20 matrix, and a bunch of things like that. And you’re like, I hope the labs aren’t training on that, because that would be kind of bizarre. In that case, we see very clean exponential progress in how many steps the models can do at a given level of reliability — say, getting the final answer right 50% of the time. And as it happens, if you take the log of the number of steps, it’s exceptionally predictive of ECI. The R² is something like 0.96, maybe even a little higher.

So you’re like, oh, maybe there’s actually one underlying thing: Can you do a long chain of steps? Or, what’s your chance on each step of making an unrecoverable mistake — one you don’t notice in a way that lets you fix it? Maybe that’s some super-generic thing that applies across loads of applications, and maybe it explains something about what’s going on.

This is all very speculative. One way in which the one-dimensional picture is clearly wrong is vision. We talked about video games — vision is a particular thing, and some models just don’t support it at all. We could run them on vision benchmarks if we wanted to, and they’d get 0%. (Actually, as we’ve discovered, on some multimodal benchmarks you can do quite well without vision, but that’s more a problem with the benchmark.) Clearly, you do actually have to train models to be good at vision; that’s a thing you can choose to do or not do. That could be the case for other capabilities too. It’s just interesting that, again, empirically, we don’t especially see it. As you say, they somehow get better at playing video games and at math at the same time, even though there’s a giant gap in human ability between those two things. We see them both go up at once.

Florian: The thing I’ve realized in the last few months, as I’m now more a part of the ecosystem, is that emergent capabilities — or big progress in new domains — are kind of fake, in the sense that there are environments, built either by the labs themselves or externally, that are needed to jumpstart progress in a domain.

From the outside, it usually looks like one of two things. Either someone creates benchmarks to showcase a gap in current model capabilities, and the labs say, “Yeah, that’s kind of true, so we should try to close that gap,” and they train the model. Or the people who train models care about a certain thing, either for their own research or for external customers — biology, for example, or life sciences in general. They train the model, and later benchmarks come out showing huge jumps between model generations. And it’s often, if not always, the case that those huge jumps happen because there was a focus on those domains.

Clara: Like robotics in Astra.

Florian: Exactly. That’s something people need to realize more, because it has a lot of implications. If you don’t train the model on wet-lab work, it will never gain those bio capabilities on its own. It has no idea how those things work.

The same applies to cyber. I’ve talked to a bunch of cybersecurity researchers, and there are two things here. One is finding bugs — finding security issues, finding all these CVEs — which is going crazy right now and is also very easy to plot in numbers. The models got better at that because they also got better at finding bugs in software generally. So the claim that models have become better and better at cybersecurity as we’ve scaled them up is true. But the claim that models have become better at offensive cybersecurity — that they’re able to hack governments or companies — that’s something that very specifically needs to be trained for. And that’s an area where, thankfully, we currently see a huge gap between open and closed models. The cybersecurity professionals I’ve talked to say there’s a stark difference because the open models aren’t persistent enough. Maybe they get through one layer, but that’s about it. The same researchers say that bug finding — finding CVEs, and exploiting them at an easy level — is something models can do. I think that’s also something you’ve found at Epoch. But there’s a huge gap in these other capabilities, and that’s something you need to train.

Alexander: We recently released some results using GLM-5.3, which at the time was probably the open-weight model best at offensive cyber and exploit development. We found that we were able to keep it working for as many tokens as we wanted, but it was lacking something. Sometimes it would have all the pieces it needed, but it couldn’t quite put them together.

Clara: Does this imply that the closed labs are just training their models really hard on offensive cyber?

Alexander: Well, one funny option — and I think you’ll agree with this, Florian — is that RL environments are kind of just like benchmarks, maybe even worse in terms of quality. So it’s probably the case that, for various reasons, lots of RL environments are effectively training models to hack. As we discussed—

Clara: Extensively, in the aftermath of the Hugging Face incident.

Alexander: Right. So maybe some very high percentage of post-training is effectively offensive cybersecurity training by accident. It’s hard to know how true that is, and I’m sure it varies by lab. I’m also sure they’re doing some deliberate stuff. It was interesting — you can decide how much you believe them — when Claude Mythos Preview came out with this giant increase in offensive cyber capabilities, Anthropic said they did not deliberately try to make it really, really good at offensive cyber. They certainly were trying to make it really, really good at software engineering, and in some sense these are software engineering tasks.

Clara: I want to get back to the question I had earlier. How much is the empirical observation that these scores are all correlated — that there’s one number that falls out of this methodology for the ECI to report — the result of a general IQ increase in models? And how much is it the result of labs buying lots of new environments and training on lots of new tasks? Because, as you said, environments and benchmarks are kind of the same thing, and the more things Epoch tests on, the more things the labs will train on.

Alexander: I think it’s a bit of both. When I actually interact with the models, they’ve clearly gotten better at explicitly reasoning through problems — System 2 kinds of things, where they’re like, “Well, what’s happening here? Let me think about the properties of this question and go through it.” That’s just a really generic way to be able to do things. So if they get better at that, I do think they can increasingly do things just by thinking about them.

But obviously, they also get trained in a bunch of RL environments. Sometimes people say labs are training models on benchmarks. I think that’s normally overblown relative to what actually happens, which is that RL environment vendors come to them and say, “Hey, we made a bunch of RL environments based on these benchmarks. Would you like to buy them?” So it’s benchmaxxing by the back door, maybe. That definitely happens, and I’m sure it plays a big role. I’m not sure I know how to disentangle those two things.

Clara: What’s the gap that would be relevant here? It has to be something like real-world performance, but it’s hard to operationalize what that distinction would be.

Alexander: One thing: sometimes we make really, really secret benchmarks. We’ve got mystery game puzzles, which are just puzzles from a game, and we’ve released no more information than that. And we still see massive performance increases. You could say the labs can just train on loads of things that are vaguely like this. But you can try to make ultra-secret, proprietary benchmarks, or you can be a really small player, so it’s very unlikely that RL environment people are deliberately targeting you. And small players still see big improvements on their stuff.

Clara: Again, the thing people care about here ultimately isn’t performance on puzzle-game benchmarks. It’s performance on real-world agentic tasks. How do you think about incorporating that into your testing?

Alexander: It’s important, but difficult. I do think it’s a really remarkable feature of the models — and maybe easy to overlook, because they’re so smart and capable and knowledgeable in so many ways — that they really, really can’t do most people’s jobs currently. There are various skills they lack, like medium- to long-term coherence and prioritization, that make them bad at this.

And it’s an interesting question whether that’s just because it’s really annoying to build RL environments for, and if we did, they’d get way better at it. That would have enormous implications — maybe we’re in a much more precarious place than we think in terms of massive employment effects coming soon. Or maybe that’s just a really, really hard skill, and there are loads of people trying really hard to teach it, but it’s really hard to get models to learn. I don’t feel like I know the answer to that very well. But clearly, the labs have a lot of incentive to do it.

Florian: My take is that society itself needs a long time to adapt, and also doesn’t want to change — which is a great thing. To be more concrete: half a year ago, the models were capable of doing these things, and everyone was talking about how you could replace all the apps in your life by coding your own. MirrorCode has shown that, yes, you kind of can; the models can do this. But no one does it, because we as humans still like to offload our responsibilities to others. We still think it’s useful for other people to take care of things. So in the end, everything kind of stays the same.

At least right now, it seems to be the same at a societal level with things like cybersecurity. There are way more good people who look at all the code, report things, catch things, and see that everything is bad, than people who try to exploit it out of evilness and inflict maximum damage. As long as that stays the same — and I’m certain it will for a long time — I’m rather hopeful about our future.

Alexander: On cybersecurity, I do think there are a lot more people who want the world to be good than who just want to cause damage. And there’s an interesting offense-defense balance question. Something I’ve found quite frustrating about the cybersecurity discourse is people saying, “Oh, it’s been ages since Mythos, and everything hasn’t been hacked yet, so I guess it’s fine.” I’m like, well, no.

As we were discussing, the open-weight models aren’t that capable at offensive cybersecurity yet. They’re still dramatically less capable than Mythos Preview was, and that was the thing that got everyone scared. So I just think we don’t know what the world’s going to be like when there are open-weight models that capable. It might be fine. Maybe the fact that defenders have even more capable models, and lots of people are working very hard on it, means it all works out. But we don’t know.

Clara: Before we wrap up, I want to tie this back to benchmarking. Presumably the ECI is a useful tool because it tells us how models perform relative to each other, and also lets us gauge the overall pace of model progress. I want to hear your general thoughts on how it’s going to fare as a tool over the next year or two, as it gets harder and harder to make these benchmarks and we start weighing more subjective factors.

I should say — maybe I should have said this earlier — that the reason I really wanted to do this discussion is that I was very surprised by the level of disagreement among smart, informed people about whether Kimi K3 had caught up to the closed frontier. I heard everything from “It’s completely the same” to “It’s eight months behind.” People really gravitated to the ECI as a way of answering this, because intuitions — even among quite smart, informed power users — were so different. My gut tells me this problem is only going to get worse, especially as we get into a situation where the use cases for which the differences are most salient are very far from what normal people use. So what’s your honest prediction for how you’re going to handle all of this?

Alexander: I’d expect, certainly over the next year, that with effort we’ll be able to keep broadly doing something like the ECI. It will probably end up changing somewhat. The benchmarks that influence most of it will probably shift toward things the models are relatively bad at, because that’s more straightforward to build benchmarks for. There will be some areas where it’s now very hard to have a good benchmark. We might figure out some answers there. But we’ll probably be able to keep doing it.

Elsewhere, we’ve seen Anthropic build their own version of the ECI for internal use, and I think we’ll probably see more people try things like that. I think how easy it is to make that go really wrong and fool yourself will probably become more of a concern. As it gets so difficult to build reasonable benchmarks, unless you’re very, very careful, it’ll be easy to accidentally include ones that are broken in various ways, and that will screw up results. We’ve started doing benchmark reviews at Epoch. I wonder if we’ll start doing ECI reviews, where we go around and say, “Actually, you have a bunch of broken benchmarks in there.”

I think it will still be a useful measure of what it always was: the ability of models on benchmarks. That will remain an interesting thing to track, but it’s quite an abstract thing to track. And it’s far from the only thing that tells you about the big, important effects of models on the world.

Slight pushback, maybe for the first time: We’ve had this coding agent revolution you were referencing, Florian, with people making their own apps. That was a giant change. It has been a giant change in software engineers’ professional experience — in what they actually do all day. You might have hoped for some metric that would have told you that was going to happen, and the ECI would not have told you. Maybe someone could have built a benchmark that showed it, but they didn’t. So we were still caught by surprise by this massive change in the practical importance of AI models, despite doing a lot to measure their abilities, particularly in software engineering. And I expect things like that will keep happening, where in some sense progress was on trend and predictable by the ECI, but surprising things were also happening in the world. Maybe we’ll look back and say, “With hindsight, we could have seen that coming.” But we didn’t.

Florian: I’d say we’ll always be able to build benchmarks that are hard for models, because if we couldn’t build those benchmarks, we also wouldn’t be able to train smarter and smarter models. We’ll always find ways, whether by broadening the scope within a certain domain or broadening our selection of domains. And if we reach a state where all benchmarks are fully saturated, then either the world should look completely different, or our benchmarks aren’t realistic enough — not good enough, or unable to capture something that’s needed for work to function.
